title: Linux fleet hardening and telemetry: CIS, auditd and eBPF
summary: Harden and watch thousands of Linux hosts: CIS baselines as code with OpenSCAP, systemd and kernel lockdown, audit rules, eBPF sensors (Falco, Tetragon), fleet patching, immutable images.
outcomes: Scan a host against a CIS profile with OpenSCAP, tailor it, and manage waivers that expire
Measure and gate systemd unit sandboxing with systemd-analyze security
Choose a kernel lockdown mode and verify sysctl values against a fleet baseline
Write keyed audit rules, read audit records with auid, and detect lost events
Explain how eBPF, Falco and Tetragon observe and enforce, and where syscall sensors go blind
Run a fleet response to an SSH vulnerability from package inventory to verified fix
Map Ebury and cryptojacking intrusions to the controls and signals that stop or reveal them

lessons.title: One host is a checklist, a fleet is a control loop

blocks.md:
In Linux for security you finished with a hardening checklist for one server: patch, expose less, SSH keys only, least privilege, logs that survive, baselines. On one machine you can log in and tick each item. Now picture 2,000 servers. Three things break.

1. You cannot log in to each one, so every setting must be applied by a program.
2. Hosts change after you harden them. **Configuration drift** is the gap that grows between how a host was set up and how it is now: an engineer edits a file during an outage, a package update ships a new default, a debug setting is never reverted.
3. You cannot watch 2,000 shells, so each host must report what happens on it to a central place.

This course answers those three problems with three questions you can ask of any fleet (a **fleet** is a group of machines run the same way):

- **What should be true?** A **baseline**: the written list of settings every host must have. You will use the public CIS Benchmarks (configuration guides from the Center for Internet Security, lesson 2) as a starting point.
- **Is it true right now?** **Assessment**: a scanner checks each host against the baseline and reports pass or fail per rule. You will run OpenSCAP, an open-source compliance scanner, for real.
- **What is happening?** **Telemetry**: a stream of security events from each host to the SIEM (security information and event management system) you met in Logging and detection engineering. You will write Linux audit rules and detections based on eBPF (small checked programs that run inside the kernel, lesson 10).

blocks.title: The fleet loop this course builds, one stage per lesson group

scenes.caption: Start from a written baseline. A config management tool turns it into the desired state and applies it to every host, not by hand.
Assessment asks whether each host still matches the baseline. Failures are drift, and they feed back into fixes.
Telemetry asks what is happening right now: which programs ran, which files changed, who did it. It flows off the host to the SIEM.
Incidents and drift both end in a change: a patch, a rebuilt image, or a better baseline. The loop never finishes; it just runs.

blocks.md:
**Desired state.** A **configuration management** tool keeps hosts at a declared state. In Ansible, an open-source automation tool that reaches hosts over SSH, you "declare the desired state of a local or remote system in your playbook" (a playbook is a YAML file of tasks). The property that makes it safe to run every hour is **idempotence**: applying it twice has the same effect as applying it once. [The Ansible docs put it plainly](https://docs.ansible.com/ansible/latest/getting_started/introduction.html): when the system is already in the described state, "Ansible does not change anything, even if the playbook runs multiple times."

Idempotence turns hardening from a one-off project into a loop: run the playbook on a schedule and drift is pulled back each time.

blocks.title: Simplified drift model: share of hosts still matching the baseline

scenes.caption: A toy model, not measured data: each week d% of still-compliant hosts drift. Hardened once with d = 3, the fleet is at 69.4% after 12 weeks and 45.3% after 26.
Re-applying the desired state every 2 weeks resets drifted settings, so compliance never falls below 94.1% in this model.
Enforce only every 13 weeks and the sawtooth dips to the same low points as before each run. How often you enforce sets the worst case.

blocks.prompt: With 3% of hosts drifting each week and no re-enforcement, roughly what share of the fleet still matches the baseline after six months (26 weeks)?
blocks.reveal: About **45%**: $0.97^{26} \approx 0.453$. Less than half the fleet, even though nobody did anything malicious. That is why this course treats hardening as a loop (enforce, assess, watch) rather than a project with an end date. The model is a simplification; real drift is lumpy, but the shape is the point.

blocks.md: A baseline you apply once decays. Write it down, apply it with an idempotent tool on a schedule, scan for drift, and stream telemetry off every host. The rest of this course fills in each box of that loop.

blocks.question: A team hardened 500 servers by hand last year using the CIS Benchmark and calls the job done. What is the main risk?
options: The CIS Benchmark is out of date after a year, so all of it is wrong
Drift: hand edits, package defaults and emergency changes have moved hosts away from the baseline, and nobody is measuring it
Hand hardening is fine as long as SSH passwords are off
Hardened hosts cannot be patched
blocks.explain: Without scheduled enforcement and assessment, hosts drift silently. The benchmark itself is updated over time, but most of last year's recommendations still apply; the problem is that nobody knows which hosts still follow them.

blocks.question: Why is idempotence the property that lets you run a hardening playbook every hour?
options: It makes the playbook run faster than a shell script
It encrypts the changes so attackers cannot see them
It guarantees the baseline itself is correct
A host already in the desired state is left unchanged, so repeated runs only fix what drifted
blocks.explain: An idempotent task checks the current state and changes only what differs. Running it again on a compliant host does nothing, which is what makes frequent enforcement safe. It says nothing about whether the baseline is a good one.

lessons.title: CIS Benchmarks: what one recommendation contains

blocks.md:
Writing a baseline from scratch means deciding hundreds of settings yourself. Most teams start from a published one instead. The most widely used for Linux are the **CIS Benchmarks** from the **Center for Internet Security (CIS)**, an independent nonprofit. CIS describes them as "prescriptive configuration recommendations" for more than 25 vendor product families (over 100 benchmarks), written through a consensus process: security professionals and subject matter experts discuss drafts on a community site, CIS WorkBench, until they reach consensus, and only then is a benchmark published. They are free to download as PDF; other formats, including the machine-readable XCCDF you will meet next lesson, are for CIS SecureSuite members.

There is one benchmark per product and version: one for Ubuntu 22.04, another for Red Hat Enterprise Linux 9, and so on, because file paths and defaults differ.

**Profiles.** Every recommendation belongs to at least one profile:

- **Level 1**: a base set that "can be implemented fairly promptly" without a big performance cost, meant to lower attack surface "while keeping machines usable".
- **Level 2**: "defense in depth" for environments where security is paramount. CIS warns these "can have an adverse effect on your organization if not implemented appropriately".
- **STIG profile**: the recommendations that match a **STIG** (security technical implementation guide), the US Department of Defense's product-specific configuration guide. It replaces what used to be Level 3.

CIS also publishes the **CIS Controls** (now v8.1), a different product: a prioritised list of security practices made of Safeguards ("each require you to do one thing"), such as keeping an asset inventory. The Controls say *what* a programme should do; a Benchmark says *how* to configure one product.

**Anatomy of one recommendation.** Each item has a number, a title, the profiles it belongs to, a description, a rationale (why it matters), an audit procedure (how to check), a remediation (how to fix), and references to other frameworks. Below is a real rule from the open-source ComplianceAsCode content for Ubuntu 22.04 (more on that project next lesson). Its references map it to CIS Ubuntu benchmark item 1.5.4 (in the benchmark version this content was built from), NIST SP 800-53 control CM-6 (configuration settings), and PCI DSS v4 requirement 3.3.1 (PCI DSS, the Payment Card Industry Data Security Standard, is the card industry's security standard for card data).

blocks.code:
Title:       Disable Core Dumps for All Users
Severity:    medium
Rationale:   A core dump includes a memory image taken at the time the
             operating system terminates an application. The memory image
             could contain sensitive data and is generally useful only for
             developers trying to debug problems.
Check:       /etc/security/limits.conf or limits.d/ contains
             *     hard   core    0
References:  CIS Ubuntu benchmark 1.5.4; NIST SP 800-53 CM-6, SC-7(10);
             PCI DSS v4 3.3.1; CIS Controls 1, 2, 7, 8, 12, 13, 15, 16
blocks.caption: Title, severity, rationale and references copied from rule disable_users_coredumps in ssg-ubuntu2204-ds.xml (ssg-debderived 0.1.71); the check line is condensed from its description. A core dump is a file holding a crashed program's memory.

blocks.title: One configuration rule, many frameworks asking for it

nodes.label:
one automated check
pass or fail

scenes.caption: An auditor for PCI, one for NIST and your own CIS baseline all ask for the same line in the same file.
So one automated check answers all of them. This is why compliance teams like mapped content: the evidence is collected once.
The flip side: a benchmark rule is only as good as its check. A host can pass the file check while a service sets its own limits at runtime.

blocks.md: Applying Level 2, or even all of Level 1, to production without testing is how hardening projects cause outages. CIS itself recommends trying the guidance in a test environment first. A benchmark is a starting point that you tailor (next lessons), not a script to run blind.

CIS Benchmarks are consensus-written, product-specific configuration baselines with Level 1, Level 2 and STIG profiles. Each recommendation has a rationale, an audit check and a remediation, and maps to other frameworks, so one automated check can serve several auditors.

blocks.question: Your company must show PCI DSS and NIST SP 800-53 evidence for 300 Ubuntu servers. Why is a mapped benchmark rule useful here?
options: One automated check of a setting produces evidence for every framework that maps to that rule
It removes the need for any auditor
PCI DSS requires the CIS Level 2 profile by name
Mapped rules are enforced by the kernel
blocks.explain: Mapped content lets one check serve several frameworks. Auditors still review the evidence, PCI DSS does not mandate a CIS profile by name, and nothing about mapping involves the kernel.

blocks.question: What is the difference between the CIS Controls and a CIS Benchmark?
options: The Controls are a prioritised list of practices for a whole programme; a Benchmark gives configuration settings for one product version
They are two names for the same document
The Controls are for Windows, the Benchmarks for Linux
Benchmarks are paid; Controls are free
blocks.explain: CIS Controls v8.1 are programme-level Safeguards (inventory, access control, logging and so on). A Benchmark is product-specific configuration guidance, such as the Ubuntu 22.04 benchmark. Benchmark PDFs are free.

lessons.title: Automating a benchmark: SCAP, OpenSCAP and ComplianceAsCode

blocks.md:
A PDF cannot check 2,000 hosts. To automate a benchmark you need it in a form a program can read. That form is **SCAP**, the **Security Content Automation Protocol** [maintained by NIST](https://csrc.nist.gov/projects/security-content-automation-protocol/specifications/xccdf) (the US National Institute of Standards and Technology): "a suite of interoperable specifications" for expressing and processing security configuration and vulnerability information. Two of its parts matter here:

- **XCCDF**, the **Extensible Configuration Checklist Description Format**: the checklist itself. It holds rules, groups them into profiles, and defines how results are stored and scored.
- **OVAL**, the **Open Vulnerability and Assessment Language**: the tests. An OVAL definition says exactly what machine state to look at (a file's contents, a package version, a sysctl value) and what counts as a match.

A single file bundling both, called a **source data stream**, is what you feed a scanner.

**The tools.** **OpenSCAP** is an open-source SCAP scanner; its command-line tool is `oscap`. The rules come from **ComplianceAsCode**, an open-source project that writes "security policy content" for Red Hat Enterprise Linux, Fedora, Ubuntu, Debian, SUSE and others, and builds it into SCAP data streams, Ansible playbooks and Bash fix scripts from the same source. Its profiles include CIS Level 1 and Level 2 for each supported distribution. Distributions package the content (on Ubuntu, in the `ssg-debderived` package).

Below is a real scan of a fresh Ubuntu 22.04 container against the CIS Level 1 Server profile.

blocks.code:
$ oscap info ssg-ubuntu2204-ds.xml | grep -A1 Title
    Title: CIS Ubuntu 22.04 Level 1 Server Benchmark
        Id: xccdf_org.ssgproject.content_profile_cis_level1_server
    ...
    Title: CIS Ubuntu 22.04 Level 2 Server Benchmark
        Id: xccdf_org.ssgproject.content_profile_cis_level2_server
    ...

$ oscap xccdf eval \
    --profile xccdf_org.ssgproject.content_profile_cis_level1_server \
    --results res.xml --report report.html ssg-ubuntu2204-ds.xml > eval.txt
$ echo $?
2
$ grep '^Result' eval.txt | sort | uniq -c
     22 Result	fail
    183 Result	notapplicable
     86 Result	pass
blocks.caption: Real run (shortened): oscap 1.2.17 on an ubuntu:22.04 Docker container, content from ssg-debderived 0.1.71. The scan of 291 rules took 26 seconds. report.html is a human-readable report; res.xml is machine-readable XCCDF results.

blocks.title: The same scan, by result

scenes.caption: 86 rules passed, 22 failed. Failures in this run were mostly PAM password rules (lockout, length, reuse), login.defs ages and umask defaults.
183 were not applicable. Many rules (or their groups) carry a platform check that applies them only to a real machine, not a container; others need a package that is not installed.
So a container scan says little about the host it runs on. Scan the hosts (or VM images) themselves, and scan container images with image tools.

blocks.md: **From fail to pass, one rule.** You can evaluate a single rule, fix it, and evaluate again. In our runs `oscap` exited with status 2 when a rule failed and 0 when all evaluated rules passed, which is what lets a pipeline or a fleet agent act on the result without parsing text.

blocks.code:
$ R=xccdf_org.ssgproject.content_rule_disable_users_coredumps
$ oscap xccdf eval --profile $P --rule $R ssg-ubuntu2204-ds.xml
Title	Disable Core Dumps for All Users
Rule	xccdf_org.ssgproject.content_rule_disable_users_coredumps
Result	fail
$ echo $?
2
$ echo '*        hard       core      0' >> /etc/security/limits.conf
$ oscap xccdf eval --profile $P --rule $R ssg-ubuntu2204-ds.xml
...
Result	pass
$ echo $?
0
blocks.caption: Real run in the same container ($P is the Level 1 Server profile id).

blocks.md: **Remediation as code.** The same content generates fixes. `oscap xccdf generate fix --fix-type ansible --profile ...` printed a playbook of over 11,000 lines for this profile. Here is the task it generated for the core dump rule. Note that it is idempotent: `lineinfile` replaces a matching line or adds one, so a second run changes nothing, and the tags tie it back to the frameworks from last lesson.

blocks.code:
- name: Disable core dumps with limits
  lineinfile:
    dest: /etc/security/limits.conf
    regexp: ^[^#].*core
    line: '*        hard       core      0'
    create: true
  when: '"libpam-runtime" in ansible_facts.packages'
  tags:
  - NIST-800-53-CM-6
  - NIST-800-53-SC-7(10)
  - PCI-DSSv4-3.3.1
  - disable_users_coredumps
  - low_complexity
  - low_disruption
  - medium_severity
  - no_reboot_needed
blocks.caption: Copied from the generated playbook. The low_disruption and no_reboot_needed tags help you choose which fixes to roll out first.

blocks.md: Running every generated fix at once on production is the fastest way to lock yourself out: the same playbook also changes PAM lockout rules, SSH ciphers and firewall policy. Generate, read, tailor, and roll out in stages (next lesson).

blocks.question: A scan of a production container returns 183 notapplicable results. What should you conclude?
options: The container is very secure
OpenSCAP is broken
Notapplicable results count as failures in CIS scoring
Many rules check machine-level settings that do not apply inside a container, so this scan says little about the host
blocks.explain: Many rules, such as those for the bootloader, partitions and mounts, apply only to a real machine in this content (a platform check detects containers), and others need packages that are absent. Scan hosts and VM images directly; a container scan is not evidence about the host.

blocks.question: Why does the exit status of `oscap xccdf eval` matter for fleet automation?
options: A script can branch on it (0 versus 2 in our runs) without parsing the text report
It encrypts the results file
It tells the kernel to reboot
It sets the profile level
blocks.explain: Machine-readable signals (the exit status, and res.xml) let a CI job, a cron wrapper or an agent mark a host non-compliant automatically. Parsing the human report is fragile.

lessons.title: Tailoring, exceptions and rolling a baseline out safely

blocks.md:
No real fleet runs a benchmark unmodified. A Kubernetes node must forward IP packets; a build server may need a debugger; a database team may need a larger core dump for a vendor case. You have three honest options for each conflict:

1. **Tailor** the profile for a whole class of hosts. The OpenSCAP manual describes a **tailoring file**, which changes "behavior of SCAP content without its direct modification": select or unselect rules, or change a variable such as minimum password length. The `autotailor` tool, part of OpenSCAP's utilities, writes one.
2. Grant a time-limited **exception** (also called a waiver) for one host: a named owner, a reason and an end date.
3. Change the system so the rule can be met.

The dishonest option, silently ignoring failures, is how dashboards end up showing 100% while hosts are wide open.

blocks.code:
# a profile for Kubernetes nodes: CIS Level 1 Server minus one rule,
# with a longer minimum password length
$ autotailor --unselect sysctl_net_ipv4_ip_forward \
             --var-value var_password_pam_minlen=16 \
             --new-profile-id cis_l1_k8s_node \
             --output k8s-node-tailoring.xml \
             ssg-ubuntu2204-ds.xml cis_level1_server
$ grep -E 'Profile id|select|set-value' k8s-node-tailoring.xml
<xccdf-1.2:Profile id="xccdf_org.ssgproject.content_profile_cis_l1_k8s_node"
    extends="xccdf_org.ssgproject.content_profile_cis_level1_server">
<xccdf-1.2:select idref="...content_rule_sysctl_net_ipv4_ip_forward" selected="false"/>
<xccdf-1.2:set-value idref="...content_value_var_password_pam_minlen">16</xccdf-1.2:set-value>

# scan with the tailored profile id, not the original one
$ oscap xccdf eval --tailoring-file k8s-node-tailoring.xml \
    --profile xccdf_org.ssgproject.content_profile_cis_l1_k8s_node \
    ssg-ubuntu2204-ds.xml | grep -c ip_forward
0
blocks.caption: Real run; XML lines shortened (...) and wrapped. autotailor from openscap-utils 1.3.9 wrote the file; oscap 1.2.17 in the Ubuntu 22.04 container used it. The unselected rule no longer appears in the results.

blocks.md: **Exceptions as data.** Keep waivers in version control next to the baseline, and make the checker read them, so an expired waiver turns back into a failure without anyone remembering. The small Python checker below compares sysctl values collected from four hosts against a baseline and a waiver list. Step through it; the outputs are from a real run.

blocks.title: A baseline check that honours waivers until they expire

scenes.caption: The baseline: four kernel settings every host must have. kptr_restrict hides kernel addresses; ip_forward = 0 means the host does not route packets.
Two waivers, each with an owner and an end date. One is still valid on 22 Nov 2026; the build-02 waiver ended on 1 Oct 2026.
Collected values. web-01 matches everything; the others differ on one or two settings.
k8s-node-07 forwards packets (got 1, want 0). A waiver covers it and is in date, so the result is WAIVED, not a silent pass.
build-02 has ptrace_scope 0. Its waiver expired in October, so waived() returns False and the host fails again automatically.
db-03 fails twice. Note unprivileged_bpf_disabled = 2: unprivileged BPF is off, but an admin may switch it back on, unlike 1. A strict check catches the weaker value.
scenes.output:
db-03        kernel.kptr_restrict              want 2 got 0 FAIL
db-03        kernel.unprivileged_bpf_disabled  want 1 got 2 FAIL

blocks.md: **Rolling out a change.** Even a correct baseline change can break something you did not test: a cipher an old client needs, a PAM lockout that hits a service account. Roll out in **rings**: a few canary hosts first (a **canary** is an early host you watch closely), then a small share of production, then everyone, scanning and watching error rates between steps. If a ring breaks, stop and roll back with the same tooling. Lesson 16 uses the same ring idea for patches.

blocks.title: A baseline change rolled out in rings (illustrative schedule)

scenes.caption: Day 0 to 2: apply the tailored profile to test hosts and run the application test suite.
Day 2 to 4: canaries in production. Scan them and watch error rates and tickets. Nothing else changes yet.
Day 4 to 6: ring 1. If something breaks, only 10% of hosts are affected and the rollback is the same playbook with the old profile.
Day 6 onward: everyone. From then on the scheduled scan reports drift against the new profile.

blocks.md: Tailor per host class, waive per host with an owner and an end date, and store both as code so an expired waiver fails on its own. Roll changes out in rings with a scan between rings.

blocks.question: An auditor finds that 40 hosts have had a failing SSH rule for a year, each with a waiver that says 'temporary, ops team'. What process fix matters most?
options: Delete the rule from the benchmark
Give every waiver an end date and a named owner, and have the checker treat expired waivers as failures
Stop scanning those 40 hosts
Move the hosts to the Level 2 profile
blocks.explain: A waiver without an expiry is a permanent silent exception. Expiry dates checked by the tool force a decision: renew with a reason, fix the host, or tailor the profile for that host class.

blocks.question: Your profile requires `kernel.unprivileged_bpf_disabled = 1`. A host reports 2. Is it compliant?
options: Yes: any non-zero value disables unprivileged BPF, so 2 is at least as strong
Yes: 2 is the stricter value
The sysctl does not exist
No: 2 also disables unprivileged BPF now, but an admin can turn it back on later, while 1 cannot be undone until reboot
blocks.explain: Both values block unprivileged bpf() today. The difference is reversibility: 1 is one-way until reboot, 2 can be changed back. Whether to accept 2 is a tailoring decision; a strict check makes you take it on purpose.

lessons.title: Measuring a service sandbox with systemd-analyze security

blocks.md:
OS security, privilege and isolation ended with one service wrapped in systemd sandboxing directives (`User=`, `NoNewPrivileges=`, `ProtectSystem=strict`, a seccomp `SystemCallFilter=` and more). On a fleet you run hundreds of different units, written by different teams. You need a way to *measure* how sandboxed each one is, and to stop a weak unit from shipping.

systemd ships that measurement. `systemd-analyze security` checks a unit's security settings, gives each missing one an "exposure" weight, and combines them into an overall **exposure level** from 0.0 (tight sandbox) to 10.0 (none). The manual is careful about what the number means: it only covers sandboxing systemd itself applies, and a high value "neither means that there is no effective sandboxing applied by the service code itself, nor that the service is actually vulnerable". It is a to-do list, not a verdict.

blocks.code:
# webd.service: the minimal unit, only ExecStart=
$ systemd-analyze security --offline=yes webd.service
  NAME                         DESCRIPTION                                        EXPOSURE
x User=/DynamicUser=           Service runs as root user                             0.4
x CapabilityBoundingSet=~CAP_SYS_TIME  Service processes may change the system clock 0.2
x NoNewPrivileges=             Service processes may acquire new privileges          0.2
ok AmbientCapabilities=        Service process does not receive ambient capabilities
x PrivateDevices=              Service potentially has access to hardware devices    0.2
x PrivateNetwork=              Service has access to the host's network              0.5
x SystemCallFilter=~@module    Service does not filter system calls                  0.2
...
Overall exposure level for webd.service: 9.4 UNSAFE :-{
blocks.caption: Real output from systemd 255 on Ubuntu 24.04, shortened and re-aligned; the tool's check and cross symbols are shown as ok and x. --offline=yes reads unit files directly, without a running systemd.

blocks.md:
**Closing the gaps.** Starting from the prereq course's unit, these directives (all in `systemd.exec(5)`) remove most of the remaining exposure. Each answers "what could an attacker inside this service still reach?":

- `ProtectKernelLogs=yes`: no access to the kernel log buffer. `ProtectClock=yes`: cannot set the clock (log timestamps stay trustworthy).
- `ProtectProc=invisible`: other users' processes are hidden from this service's `/proc`.
- `PrivateDevices=yes`: a private `/dev` with only pseudo devices like `/dev/null`, no disks or `/dev/mem`.

- `RestrictAddressFamilies=AF_INET AF_INET6 AF_UNIX`: no raw packet or netlink sockets.
- `RestrictSUIDSGID=yes`: cannot create setuid or setgid files.
- `MemoryDenyWriteExecute=yes`: no memory that is both writable and executable (breaks programs with JIT compilers, so test).
- `SystemCallArchitectures=native`: only the native system call ABI, so a 32-bit call path cannot slip past the filter (lesson 8 shows the same trap in audit rules).
- `IPAddressDeny=any` plus `IPAddressAllow=10.0.0.0/8`: network traffic limited to the internal range.

blocks.code:
[Service]
ExecStart=/usr/local/bin/webd
User=webd
AmbientCapabilities=CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE
CapabilityBoundingSet=CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE
NoNewPrivileges=yes
ProtectSystem=strict
ProtectHome=yes
PrivateTmp=yes
ReadWritePaths=/var/lib/webd
ProtectKernelModules=yes
ProtectKernelTunables=yes
ProtectKernelLogs=yes
ProtectControlGroups=yes
ProtectClock=yes
ProtectHostname=yes
ProtectProc=invisible
PrivateDevices=yes
RestrictNamespaces=yes
RestrictAddressFamilies=AF_INET AF_INET6 AF_UNIX
RestrictRealtime=yes
RestrictSUIDSGID=yes
LockPersonality=yes
MemoryDenyWriteExecute=yes
SystemCallArchitectures=native
SystemCallFilter=@system-service
SystemCallFilter=~@privileged @resources
SystemCallErrorNumber=EPERM
UMask=0077
IPAddressDeny=any
IPAddressAllow=10.0.0.0/8
blocks.caption: webd3.service: the prereq unit (webd2), the additions above, and a few small ones: ProtectControlGroups and ProtectHostname (cgroups, hostname read-only), RestrictRealtime, LockPersonality, UMask=0077, and a second SystemCallFilter line removing @privileged and @resources.

blocks.title: Exposure level of the same service, three unit files (real scores)

scenes.caption: Only ExecStart=: the service runs as root with every capability and every system call. Exposure 9.4, rated UNSAFE.
The prereq course's unit (own user, one capability, read-only system, seccomp allow-list) drops it to 3.6.
Adding the directives above gives 1.3. What is left is mostly by design: it binds a port with one ambient capability and uses the network.

blocks.md: **Make it a gate.** With `--offline=yes`, the `--threshold=` option makes the command fail when a unit is more exposed than you allow. The threshold is on a 0 to 100 scale (the default 100 never fails), so `--threshold=50` rejects anything above 5.0. Run it in the pipeline that builds your packages or images, and a new unit with no sandboxing never reaches the fleet.

blocks.code:
$ for u in webd webd2 webd3; do
>   systemd-analyze security --offline=yes --threshold=50 $u.service >/dev/null 2>&1
>   echo "$u exit=$?"
> done
webd exit=1
webd2 exit=0
webd3 exit=0
blocks.caption: Real run. Exit 1 fails a CI job; 0 lets it pass.

blocks.prompt: You add `PrivateNetwork=yes` to webd3 to bring the score even lower. What happens to the web service?
blocks.reveal: It stops serving clients. `PrivateNetwork=yes` gives the service its own network namespace with only a loopback interface, so it cannot reach or be reached by the host's network. The exposure score improves (the tool weighs host network access at 0.5), which shows why the number is a to-do list: some items are exactly what the service exists to do.

blocks.md: Every directive can break something: `MemoryDenyWriteExecute` breaks JIT runtimes, `ProtectProc=invisible` can break tools that inspect other processes, `ProcSubset=pid` is, per the manual, not suitable for most non-trivial programs. Add directives one at a time on a test host and watch the journal for denials.

`systemd-analyze security` turns sandboxing into a number you can track per unit and gate in CI with `--offline=yes --threshold=`. Lower is better, but the score covers only systemd's own settings and cannot tell you what the service legitimately needs.

blocks.question: A team's unit scores 2.1 and another's scores 7.8. Which statement is justified by the tool's documentation?
options: The 7.8 service is vulnerable and must be shut down
The 2.1 service cannot be exploited
Both scores measure the service's CVE count
The 7.8 service applies little systemd sandboxing and would likely benefit from more directives; neither score says whether the code is vulnerable
blocks.explain: The manual says high exposure means little sandboxing applied by systemd, not that the service is vulnerable, and it ignores sandboxing done inside the program. It is a prioritised to-do list.

blocks.question: Why does `SystemCallArchitectures=native` matter for a seccomp filter on x86-64?
options: It speeds up system calls
It blocks the 32-bit system call interface, whose call numbers differ, so a process cannot use that path to avoid filters written for 64-bit numbers
It disables all networking
It is required for ProtectSystem to work
blocks.explain: x86-64 Linux also accepts 32-bit system calls with a different numbering. Allowing only the native ABI closes that second door. Audit rules need the same care: rules for both arch=b64 and arch=b32 (lesson 8).

lessons.title: Kernel lockdown modes and sysctl baselines across a fleet

blocks.md:
The prereq course introduced **kernel lockdown** (an LSM, a Linux Security Module, added in Linux 5.4) that stops even root from modifying the running kernel, and a list of hardening `sysctl` values. On a fleet you have to choose a lockdown *mode*, and that choice collides with your own security tools.

The kernel's boot parameter documentation defines two modes. `lockdown=integrity` disables "kernel features that allow userland to modify the running kernel". `lockdown=confidentiality` also disables features "that allow userland to extract confidential information from the kernel". The source code shows how: every restricted feature has a numbered reason, and one comparison decides.

blocks.title: How the kernel decides what lockdown blocks

scenes.caption: Each restricted feature is a numbered reason (numbers from current mainline). Reasons below INTEGRITY_MAX protect the kernel from being changed; those between it and CONFIDENTIALITY_MAX protect kernel secrets from being read.
Integrity mode stores level 21. A request to load an unsigned module checks reason 1: 21 >= 1, so it is refused and logged.
scenes.output: Lockdown: insmod: unsigned module loading is restricted; see man kernel_lockdown.7

scenes.caption: In the same mode, an eBPF sensor attaching a kprobe checks reason 23: 21 >= 23 is false, so it is allowed. Integrity mode leaves tracing working.
Confidentiality mode stores 30. Now kprobes (23) and BPF reads of kernel memory (24) are refused too, which breaks most eBPF security sensors.
Switching modes at runtime goes through lock_kernel_down(). Asking for a lower level fails: root can raise lockdown, never lower it, until reboot.

blocks.md:
**Reading the mode.** The current mode is in securityfs (a small pseudo-filesystem at /sys/kernel/security where security modules expose their settings); the active one is in brackets, so `[integrity]` below means integrity mode is on. Writing a higher level name to the file raises it.

**Choosing.** Bottlerocket, an open-source Linux distribution for hosting containers built at Amazon, documents that it enables lockdown in integrity mode on most variants, and sets it to none on GPU variants that must load unsigned kernel modules. Integrity is the usual fleet choice: it blocks rootkit modules, `/dev/mem` writes and unsigned `kexec`, while leaving the kprobes and BPF reads your telemetry needs. Confidentiality fits machines that hold secrets in kernel memory and run no tracing-based sensors.

blocks.code:
$ cat /sys/kernel/security/lockdown
none [integrity] confidentiality

# choose at boot (kernel command line)
lockdown=integrity
module.sig_enforce=1
blocks.caption: Format of the securityfs file from lockdown_read() in the kernel source (illustrative, not run here: the Docker Desktop kernel used for this course has no lockdown LSM).

blocks.md:
**sysctl at fleet scale: who wins?** Hardening values live in files under `/etc/sysctl.d`, but packages also ship files in `/usr/lib/sysctl.d`. `sysctl.d(5)` sets the rules: all files from all directories are sorted by file name, and when two files set the same key, the file whose name sorts **last** wins. A file in `/etc` replaces a file with the *same name* in `/usr/lib`. The manual recommends numbers 60 to 90 for administrator files in `/etc`.

So a vendor package dropping `99-vendor.conf` into `/usr/lib/sysctl.d` silently overrides your `60-hardening.conf`. The fix is to check the running value in `/proc/sys`, not the file you wrote.

blocks.title: Which file sets kernel.kptr_restrict? (sorted by name, last wins)

scenes.caption: Three files set kptr_restrict: a distribution default, your hardening file in /etc, and a vendor file. sysctl reads them in name order.
Your 60-hardening.conf sets 2 and overrides the default 1. If that were the last file, the baseline would hold.
But 99-vendor.conf sorts later, so its 0 wins, even though it lives in /usr. The kernel runs with addresses exposed, and your file still says 2.
Fix: name your file so it sorts last (or override 99-vendor.conf by the same name in /etc), then verify with sysctl kernel.kptr_restrict on every host.

blocks.code:
# what the running kernel says (Docker Desktop's Linux VM, Nov 2026)
$ sysctl kernel.kptr_restrict kernel.unprivileged_bpf_disabled \
         kernel.modules_disabled kernel.io_uring_disabled
kernel.kptr_restrict = 0
kernel.unprivileged_bpf_disabled = 0
kernel.modules_disabled = 0
kernel.io_uring_disabled = 0
blocks.caption: Real output from the VM used to build this course: a developer kernel with none of the prereq course's hardening values. A fleet scan would flag every line.

blocks.md: One new knob for this course: `kernel.io_uring_disabled`. **io_uring** is a Linux interface for asynchronous input and output in which a program places requests in ring buffers shared with the kernel instead of making one system call per operation. [Per the kernel docs](https://docs.kernel.org/admin-guide/sysctl/kernel.html), setting 1 stops unprivileged processes outside `io_uring_group` from creating io_uring instances, and 2 stops all processes; the docs say this "shrinks the kernel's attack surface". Lesson 13 shows why it also matters for telemetry.

Use lockdown integrity mode on fleets that run eBPF or kprobe sensors; confidentiality also blocks the reads those sensors need. Lockdown only ever goes up until reboot. For sysctl, the last-sorted file wins across directories, so always verify running values, not config files.

blocks.question: Your EDR's eBPF sensor stops working after a hardening change. Which change most likely caused it?
options: lockdown=integrity on the kernel command line
module.sig_enforce=1
lockdown=confidentiality on the kernel command line
kernel.kptr_restrict = 1
blocks.explain: Confidentiality mode also refuses kprobes (reason 23) and BPF reads of kernel memory (reason 24), which tracing-based sensors depend on. Integrity mode allows them; module signing affects only modules.

blocks.question: You ship /etc/sysctl.d/60-hardening.conf with kernel.yama.ptrace_scope = 1. A host reports 0. A package installed /usr/lib/sysctl.d/90-debug.conf setting it to 0. Why does the package win?
options: Files in /usr always beat files in /etc
The kernel ignores files in /etc/sysctl.d
All files are sorted by name across directories and the last one to set a key wins; 90-debug sorts after 60-hardening
ptrace_scope cannot be set from a file
blocks.explain: sysctl.d(5): files are sorted lexicographically regardless of directory, and the latest name wins for a repeated key. /etc only wins over a file with the same name. Rename yours to sort later or override 90-debug.conf by name.

blocks.question: An intruder with root runs `echo none > /sys/kernel/security/lockdown` on a host booted with lockdown=integrity. What happens?
options: Lockdown is turned off until reboot
The host reboots
Lockdown switches to confidentiality
The write fails: lock_kernel_down() refuses any level lower than the current one
blocks.explain: lock_kernel_down() returns -EPERM when the current level is already at or above the requested one, and none (0) is below integrity (21). Only a reboot with different parameters lowers it, which is why boot integrity (Secure Boot) matters.

lessons.title: The Linux audit system: how a system call becomes a record

blocks.md:
journald and auth.log (from Linux for security) record what programs *choose* to log. An intruder's own commands log nothing. The **Linux audit system** records from inside the kernel instead: when a system call matches a rule, the kernel writes a record whatever the program wanted. It is the oldest built-in source of Linux security telemetry, and benchmark audit sections (CIS included) are written for it.

Three parts:

- The **kernel audit subsystem** evaluates rules at system call exit and builds records.
- **auditd**, "the userspace component to the Linux Auditing System", reads records from the kernel over an audit netlink socket (a kernel-to-program message channel) and writes them to `/var/log/audit/audit.log`. It can also pass them to **plugins** configured in `/etc/audit/plugins.d/`, for example to forward them.
- Tools: `auditctl` loads rules and shows status, `ausearch` finds events, `aureport` summarises them.

blocks.title: One command, from system call to log line

scenes.caption: A shell runs su alice -c id. The new process calls execve(), the system call that starts a program.
At system call exit the kernel checks the loaded rules. An execve rule matches, so it builds several records that share one event id.
The records go through the audit netlink socket to auditd, which writes them to disk.
A plugin or a log shipper sends the same records off the host. Once they have left, root on this host cannot unwrite them.

blocks.md: **One event, several records.** Here is that exact event as auditd stored it, captured from a real run. Every line starts with a record `type=` and `msg=audit(TIME:SERIAL)`. TIME is seconds since 1 January 1970 (Unix time) and SERIAL is the event number; lines with the same pair belong to the same event. With `log_format = ENRICHED` (the Ubuntu default) auditd appends resolved names in capitals after the raw numbers.

blocks.code:
type=SYSCALL msg=audit(1795411850.553:7): arch=c00000b7 syscall=221 success=yes
  exit=0 ... ppid=66685 pid=66699 auid=1001 uid=0 gid=0 euid=0 ... ses=2
  comm="su" exe="/usr/bin/su" key="user_exec"ARCH=aarch64 SYSCALL=execve
  AUID="alice" UID="root" ...
type=EXECVE msg=audit(1795411850.553:7): argc=4 a0="su" a1="alice" a2="-c" a3="id"
type=CWD msg=audit(1795411850.553:7): cwd="/"
type=PATH msg=audit(1795411850.553:7): item=0 name="/usr/bin/su" inode=545174
  dev=00:45 mode=0104755 ouid=0 ogid=0 ...
type=PROCTITLE msg=audit(1795411850.553:7): proctitle=737500616C696365002D63006964
blocks.caption: Real records from auditd 3.1.2 on Ubuntu 24.04 (arm64), wrapped and shortened with ... . mode=0104755 is a regular file with the setuid bit. uid=0 here because the demo shell was already root; setuid changes only the effective uid (euid), so alice running su would log uid=1001 euid=0.

blocks.md:
**Reading it.**

- **SYSCALL** says which call (`syscall=221` is execve on this 64-bit Arm machine; the number differs per architecture), whether it succeeded, the process and parent ids, the identities, the executable and the rule `key`.
- **EXECVE** holds the arguments, **CWD** the working directory, **PATH** one line per file the call touched, with owner and mode.
- **PROCTITLE** is the full command line, hex-encoded; inside, the arguments are separated by zero bytes. You decode it yourself or let `ausearch -i` do it.

The field that makes audit special is **auid**, the audit user id or **login uid**. `uid=0` says the process runs as root (here because the demo shell was root); `auid=1001` says which human logged in to start this chain. [The `pam_loginuid` module](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man8/pam_loginuid.8.html) "sets the loginuid process attribute for the process that was authenticated" at entry points like login and sshd, and its manual warns not to use it for sudo or su, because they must *keep* the original. So auid survives every su and sudo: the record still says alice. (In this demo container there was no SSH login, so we set the login uid by hand, as pam_loginuid would.)

blocks.code:
import re

line = 'type=PROCTITLE msg=audit(1795411850.553:7): proctitle=737500616C696365002D63006964'
stamp, serial = re.search(r"audit\((\d+\.\d+):(\d+)\)", line).groups()
raw = bytes.fromhex(line.split("proctitle=")[1])
print("time  ", stamp, " event", serial)
print("bytes ", raw)
print("argv  ", raw.split(b"\x00"))

# output (real run):
# time   1795411850.553  event 7
# bytes  b'su\x00alice\x00-c\x00id'
# argv   [b'su', b'alice', b'-c', b'id']
blocks.caption: Decoding PROCTITLE in Python. The bytes are the argument list joined by zero bytes.

blocks.title: auid stays with the human while uid and euid change

scenes.caption: Before login, sshd runs as root and has no login uid yet (unset, printed as 4294967295).
pam_loginuid sets the login uid when alice authenticates. Alice's shell runs with uid and euid 1001 and auid 1001.
Alice runs su -c id. su is setuid root, so its euid becomes 0 while its real uid stays 1001 (its audit record says uid=1001 euid=0). auid stays 1001.
After the root password check, su switches every id to root and starts sh, which runs id. Both log uid=0 euid=0, yet auid is still 1001: every root record names alice.

blocks.md: The demo machine's earlier records show `auid=4294967295` (unset) for processes started by the container runtime: nothing ever logged in. On a fleet, activity with an unset auid is normal for daemons and suspicious for interactive commands.

Audit records come from the kernel, not the program, and one event is several records sharing TIME:SERIAL. auid (the login uid) is set once at login and survives su and sudo, which is what lets you attribute root actions to a person.

blocks.question: A record shows `uid=0 auid=1004 comm="cat" exe="/usr/bin/cat"` reading /etc/shadow. What does it tell you?
options: Root logged in directly and read the file
cat has a setuid bug
The user with uid 1004 logged in and, through su or sudo, is now running cat as root
The record is corrupt because uid and auid differ
blocks.explain: uid is the real user id, which becomes 0 only after su or sudo switches user (a setuid program alone changes euid); auid is who logged in. Different values are exactly what you expect after su or sudo, and they let you name the person.

blocks.question: Why should pam_loginuid not be added to the PAM stack of sudo?
options: It would slow sudo down
sudo does not use PAM
It would disable auditd
sudo would set the login uid to the target account (root), erasing the record of who actually logged in
blocks.explain: Its manual says to use it only at entry points (login, sshd, cron) because on su or sudo it would change the loginuid to the account switched to, which "defeats the purpose".

lessons.title: Writing audit rules that answer real questions

blocks.md:
An audit rule should answer a question an investigator will ask: *who changed sudoers?*, *what did this person run as root?*, *was a kernel module loaded?*. `audit.rules(7)` describes three kinds of rule:

- **Control** rules configure the system: `-D` deletes all rules, `-b` sets the kernel backlog, `-f` the failure mode, `-e` the enabled flag.
- **File** rules, or **watches**: `-w /etc/sudoers -p wa -k priv_esc` records writes (`w`) and attribute changes (`a`) to that path. `r` and `x` (read, execute) also exist. A watch on a directory covers the tree below it.
- **System call** rules: `-a always,exit -F arch=b64 -S execve -F auid>=1000 -F auid!=unset -k user_exec`. `-a always,exit` appends to the exit list with action always; `-S` names system calls; each `-F` adds a field test, and all tests must be true.

`-k` attaches a **key**, a free-text tag copied into every matching record. The manual's "best advice is to use keys": during an investigation you start from `aureport --key --summary` and drill down with `ausearch -k`.

blocks.code:
## /etc/audit/rules.d/50-fleet.rules
## who changed identity or privilege files
-w /etc/passwd -p wa -k identity
-w /etc/shadow -p wa -k identity
-w /etc/sudoers -p wa -k priv_esc
-w /etc/sudoers.d/ -p wa -k priv_esc
## persistence locations
-w /etc/systemd/system/ -p wa -k persistence
-w /etc/cron.d/ -p wa -k persistence
-w /etc/ld.so.preload -p wa -k preload
## kernel modules loaded or removed
-a always,exit -F arch=b64 -S init_module,finit_module,delete_module -k modules
## every program started by a logged-in human
-a always,exit -F arch=b64 -S execve -F auid>=1000 -F auid!=unset -k user_exec
blocks.caption: The persistence lines map to ATT&CK techniques you met in Linux for security: systemd services (T1543.002), cron (T1053.003) and /etc/ld.so.preload (T1574.006, dynamic linker hijacking), which makes every program load a listed library first.

blocks.md: **Two traps in that last rule.** First, `auid>=1000` alone would also match unset processes, because unset is stored as 4294967295, a very large number; the manual's own example adds `auid!=unset` for exactly this reason (1000 is where human accounts start, per `UID_MIN` in `/etc/login.defs`). Second, on 64-bit x86, programs can also make 32-bit system calls, whose numbers sometimes differ. A rule with only `arch=b64` never sees the 32-bit path, so the manual says to write each syscall rule twice, once with `-F arch=b32` and once with `-F arch=b64`. (The demo machine is 64-bit Arm, where we used b64 only.)

blocks.code:
$ auditctl -R /etc/audit/rules.d/50-fleet.rules
$ auditctl -l
-w /etc/passwd -p wa -k identity
...
-a always,exit -F arch=b64 -S init_module,delete_module,finit_module -F key=modules
-a always,exit -F arch=b64 -S execve -F auid>=1000 -F auid!=-1 -F key=user_exec

# a short intrusion story, run with login uid 1001 (alice) as root
cp /tmp/u/webd.service /etc/systemd/system/updater.service
echo "*/5 * * * * root /usr/local/bin/updater" > /etc/cron.d/updater
touch /etc/ld.so.preload
useradd -r svc-backup

$ aureport -k --summary
Key Summary Report
===========================
total  key
===========================
10  user_exec
4  identity
2  persistence
1  preload
blocks.caption: Real run in an Ubuntu 24.04 container (auditd 3.1.2). auditctl prints unset as -1. The script produced 17 keyed events; useradd alone wrote 4 identity events (opening and renaming passwd and shadow).

blocks.code:
$ ausearch -k persistence -i | grep -E '^type=(SYSCALL|PROCTITLE)'
type=PROCTITLE ... : proctitle=cp /tmp/u/webd.service /etc/systemd/system/updater.service
type=SYSCALL ... : arch=aarch64 syscall=openat success=yes ... auid=alice uid=root
  ... comm=cp exe=/usr/bin/cp key=persistence
type=PROCTITLE ... : proctitle=bash /tmp/story.sh
type=SYSCALL ... : arch=aarch64 syscall=openat success=yes ... auid=alice uid=root
  ... comm=bash exe=/usr/bin/bash key=persistence
blocks.caption: Real output, shortened. The cron file was written by a shell redirection, so the writing process is bash itself; the command line shows the script that ran it.

blocks.md:
**Order and the never action.** Syscall rules sit in lists, and in auditctl's words "the event triggers on the first matching rule". So a `never` rule that suppresses noise must come *before* the broad rule it carves out of; placed after, it never takes effect. Every syscall rule is also evaluated for every system call of every program, so the manual's performance advice is: few syscall rules, combine syscalls into one rule when the fields are identical, and always give `arch`.

The toy model below shows first-match evaluation. It is a simplification written for this course, not audit's code.

blocks.title: First matching rule wins (toy model, real output)
blocks.code:
# toy model of the audit exit filter: rules are checked top-down,
# the first rule whose fields all match decides
UNSET = 4294967295
rules = [
    ("never",  {"exe": "/usr/sbin/cron-helper"},                 None),
    ("always", {"syscall": "execve", "auid>=": 1000, "auid!=": UNSET}, "user_exec"),
    ("always", {"syscall": "execve"},                          "all_exec"),
]

def matches(fields, ev):
    for name, want in fields.items():
        if name == "auid>=" and not ev["auid"] >= want: return False
        if name == "auid!=" and not ev["auid"] != want: return False
        if name in ("exe", "syscall") and ev[name] != want: return False
    return True

def decide(ev):
    for action, fields, key in rules:
        if matches(fields, ev):
            return action, key
    return "no rule", None

events = [
    {"syscall": "execve", "exe": "/usr/bin/id",           "auid": 1001},
    {"syscall": "execve", "exe": "/usr/sbin/cron-helper", "auid": 1001},
    {"syscall": "execve", "exe": "/usr/sbin/nginx",       "auid": UNSET},
    {"syscall": "openat", "exe": "/usr/bin/cat",          "auid": 1001},
]
for ev in events:
    print(ev["exe"], ev["auid"], ":", *decide(ev))

scenes.caption: Three rules, top to bottom: drop a noisy helper, record humans' commands with key user_exec, record all other execs with key all_exec.
alice (auid 1001) runs id. Rule 1 does not match the exe; rule 2 matches all three fields and decides.
The noisy helper matches rule 1 first, so no record is written even though rule 2 would also match. Put never rules on top.
nginx started at boot has auid unset (4294967295). That passes auid>=1000 but fails auid!=unset, so rule 2 is skipped and rule 3 records it.
openat matches no rule, so nothing is recorded. Rules decide what exists in your logs later; nothing else will.

blocks.md:
**Managing rules on a fleet.** Ship rules as files in `/etc/audit/rules.d/` and [let **augenrules** merge them](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man8/augenrules.8.html): it concatenates files ending in `.rules` in natural sort order into `/etc/audit/audit.rules`, and always moves the last `-D` to the top and the last `-e` to the bottom.

The bottom line in production is usually `-e 2`. In auditctl's words, it locks the configuration "so that it can't be changed"; any attempt "will be audited and denied", and only a reboot unlocks it. That stops an intruder with root from quietly deleting your rules, at the price that you also need a reboot to change them.

`-w` watches are the older syntax; audit.rules(7) calls them deprecated and slower, recommending `-a always,exit -F arch=b64 -F path=... -F perm=wa` instead. Many published baselines still use `-w`, and both work. And remember the limit: audit sees system calls. Lesson 13 shows activity that never makes one.

Write rules for questions, give every rule a key, use auid>=1000 together with auid!=unset, write b32 and b64 rules on x86-64, put never rules first, keep syscall rules few, and end production rule sets with -e 2.

blocks.question: You add `-a never,exit -F arch=b64 -S execve -F exe=/usr/bin/backup-agent` at the end of your rules to stop its noise, but its events keep appearing. Why?
options: never rules only work on the user list
exe= is not a valid field
The broad execve rule above it matches first, and the first matching rule decides
auditd ignores never rules unless -e 2 is set
blocks.explain: auditctl says events trigger on the first matching rule, so suppressions belong at the top. Move the never rule above the broad execve rule.

blocks.question: On an x86-64 server your only execve rule is `-F arch=b64 -S execve`. What can an attacker do?
options: Nothing: b64 covers every call on a 64-bit kernel
Disable auditd without root
Run programs through the 32-bit system call interface, which this rule never evaluates
Read your rules file
blocks.explain: The 32-bit ABI has its own syscall numbers and audit evaluates it separately. Add the same rule with -F arch=b32 (and consider SystemCallArchitectures=native for services, lesson 5).

blocks.question: Why is `-e 2` placed as the last rule rather than the first?
options: It makes auditd start faster
It locks the configuration, so every rule must already be loaded before it runs
augenrules requires it alphabetically
It enables the b32 rules
blocks.explain: Once the configuration is locked, no rule can be added or removed until reboot. Rules after it would fail to load. augenrules moves the last -e to the bottom for this reason.

lessons.title: When audit falls behind: backlog, lost events and full disks

blocks.md:
Rules decide what *should* be recorded. Whether it actually reaches your SIEM depends on a queue, a disk and a network, and each can fail under load or under attack.

**The kernel backlog.** Records wait in a kernel queue until auditd reads them. `auditctl -b` sets its limit, the **backlog limit** (the kernel default is 64; Ubuntu's packaged rules raise it to 8192 with the comment "Make this bigger for busy systems"). When the queue is full, the kernel waits up to `--backlog_wait_time` for room and then consults the **failure flag** (`-f`): 0 silent, 1 printk (write a kernel log message, the default), 2 **panic** (halt the machine). The manual says "Secure environments will probably want to set this to 2". Records the kernel had to drop are counted in the **lost** counter of `auditctl -s`.

blocks.code:
$ auditctl -s
enabled 1
failure 1
pid 71249
rate_limit 0
backlog_limit 64
lost 3
backlog 0
backlog_wait_time 60000
backlog_wait_time_actual 0
loginuid_immutable 0 unlocked

# experiment: pause auditd, then start 300 programs as a logged-in user
$ auditctl --reset-lost; auditctl -b 64 --backlog_wait_time 0
$ kill -STOP $(pidof auditd)
$ for i in $(seq 1 300); do /bin/true; done
$ auditctl -s | grep -E '^(backlog_limit|lost|backlog) '
backlog_limit 64
lost 262
backlog 65
$ dmesg | grep audit | tail -3
audit: audit_lost=3 audit_rate_limit=0 audit_backlog_limit=64
audit: backlog limit exceeded
audit: audit_backlog=65 > audit_backlog_limit=64
blocks.caption: Real run, user_exec rule from lesson 8 loaded, kernel 6.12. With failure 1 the only traces are the counter and a rate-limited kernel message (so dmesg shows only the first losses, audit_lost=3). The wait time was set to 0 so the loop would not stall; by default the kernel waits for room.

blocks.title: Simplified queue model: seconds until a full backlog during a burst

scenes.caption: A toy model: records arrive faster than auditd drains them, and the backlog absorbs the difference. At 2,000 arriving and 1,500 drained per second, 8,192 slots last 16.4 seconds.
With the kernel default of 64 slots the same burst fills the queue in 0.13 seconds. Our experiment above was the extreme case: auditd was paused and drained nothing.
A bigger backlog buys time, not capacity. If arrival stays above the drain rate the queue fills anyway, so the real fixes are fewer noisy rules and a faster consumer.

blocks.md:
**The disk.** auditd's own settings in `auditd.conf(5)` decide what happens as its partition fills: `space_left_action`, `admin_space_left_action`, `disk_full_action` and `disk_error_action` can ignore, log to syslog, rotate, suspend logging, switch to single-user mode, or halt. Ubuntu 24.04's packaged defaults include `max_log_file_action = ROTATE` with `num_logs = 5`, `space_left_action = SYSLOG`, and `SUSPEND` for the admin-space, disk-full and disk-error cases, which means auditd *stops writing* when the disk is full. The manual's guidance for strict environments is the opposite: `single` or `halt` when the disk is full, because "no more audit capability exists".

That is the core trade-off of audit on a fleet: **completeness versus availability**. Panic and halt guarantee nothing happens unrecorded, at the cost of taking production down on a log storm. Most fleets keep printk and suspend, and instead *alert* on the signals of loss.

blocks.title: Where audit data is lost, and the signal each loss leaves

nodes.label:
alerts on: lost > 0,
auditd down, host silent

scenes.caption: Loss point 1: the backlog fills. Signal: the lost counter rises and the kernel logs 'backlog limit exceeded'.
Loss point 2: auditd is stopped or killed. Root can do this. Signal: no audit records from that host, and an exec of auditctl or kill seen just before.
Loss point 3: the disk fills and auditd suspends, or someone deletes audit.log. Records already shipped off the host survive.
Defend the pipeline itself: collect auditctl -s lost values, alert when a host goes quiet, and forward continuously so deletion on the host does not erase the record.

blocks.md: **Attackers know this too.** MITRE ATT&CK's entry for TeamTNT, a cryptomining group you will meet in lesson 15, records that it "removed system logs from /var/log/syslog" and "cleared command history with history -c". ATT&CK files clearing Linux system logs under T1685.006, Clear Linux or Mac System Logs (formerly T1070.002). Local logs are evidence only until the intruder gets root; shipped logs, plus an alert when a host stops sending, are what survive.

Size the backlog for bursts (8192 is the packaged default on Ubuntu), choose the failure and disk actions deliberately (availability versus completeness), ship records off the host continuously, and alert on lost > 0 and on hosts that go silent.

blocks.question: `auditctl -s` on a busy host shows `lost 18402` and `failure 1`. What happened?
options: auditd lost its configuration file
18402 rules failed to load
An attacker set -e 2
The kernel backlog filled at some point and the kernel dropped records, writing only a kernel log message because the failure mode is printk
blocks.explain: lost counts records discarded because the kernel queue overflowed (or similar critical errors). With failure 1 the kernel prints a message and continues. Find the noisy rule, raise the backlog, or speed up the consumer.

blocks.question: A bank's audit requirement says no security-relevant action may happen unrecorded. Which settings match that requirement, and what is the cost?
options: -f 0 and disk_full_action = ignore; no cost
-f 1 and disk_full_action = suspend; the host may halt
-f 2 and disk_full_action = halt; the host stops (panic or halt) rather than run unaudited, so a log storm becomes an outage
-e 0; audit is temporarily disabled
blocks.explain: Panic on audit failure and halt on a full disk guarantee nothing runs unrecorded, which is what the manual suggests for secure environments. The price is availability, so pair them with generous disk, rotation and alerting on space_left.

lessons.title: eBPF: small verified programs that watch the kernel from inside

blocks.md:
Audit gives you fixed record types, filtered by a fixed rule language, delivered through one queue. Modern Linux sensors mostly use **eBPF** instead. The eBPF project describes it as technology that can "run sandboxed programs in a privileged context such as the operating system kernel", extending the kernel "without requiring to change kernel source code or load kernel modules". BPF originally stood for **Berkeley Packet Filter** (the e in eBPF is for extended), a mechanism for filtering network packets; the eBPF site says that now that eBPF does far more, "the acronym no longer makes sense" and eBPF is a name in its own right.

The idea in one sentence: you write a small function, the kernel checks it is safe, and then runs it every time a chosen event happens, inside the kernel, with access to the kernel's own view of that event.

blocks.title: Loading and running one eBPF program

scenes.caption: The sensor compiles a small program to eBPF bytecode and loads it with the bpf() system call. Only root or a process with CAP_BPF (plus CAP_PERFMON for tracing programs) may do this, unless unprivileged eBPF is enabled.
The verifier walks every path: the program must always finish and must not touch memory it is not allowed to. Then the JIT compiler turns it into machine code.
The program is attached to a hook: a tracepoint, a kprobe on a kernel function, an LSM hook, or a network event.
Each time the event fires, the program runs in the kernel, filters, and writes only what matters into a map or ring buffer that the sensor reads.

blocks.md:
**The parts, from the eBPF documentation.**

- **Hooks.** Programs are event-driven. Predefined hooks include system calls, function entry and exit, kernel **tracepoints** (stable, named instrumentation points), and network events. Where none exists you can create a **kprobe** (a kernel probe on almost any kernel function) or a **uprobe** (the same for a user program). The kernel also offers **LSM BPF** programs attached to Linux Security Module hooks, which can not only observe a check but return an error such as `-EPERM` to deny it.
- **Verifier.** Every program passes it. Programs must run to completion (loops only if bounded) and stay within a complexity limit. The docs stress it is "a safety tool, checking that programs are safe to run. It is not a security tool inspecting what the programs are doing."
- **JIT.** A just-in-time compiler turns bytecode into native instructions, so programs run about as fast as kernel code.
- **Maps.** Shared data structures, readable from both the program and user space; this is how events and counters leave the kernel.

**A real tracer in four lines.** bpftrace is a high-level tracing language for eBPF, inspired by awk and C. This program attaches to the `sched_process_exec` tracepoint, which fires whenever a process successfully starts a new program, and prints who ran what. Note `su` at uid 0: the demo shell was already root, as in lesson 7. bpftrace's `uid` is the real user id, so a setuid program started by alice would still show 1001 here; only its effective uid becomes 0.

blocks.code:
$ cat exec.bt
tracepoint:sched:sched_process_exec
{
  printf("uid=%d pid=%d comm=%s file=%s\n", uid, pid, comm, str(args->filename));
}
$ bpftrace exec.bt          # in another shell: su alice -c "id; cat /etc/hostname"
Attaching 1 probe...
uid=0 pid=66631 comm=su file=/usr/bin/su
uid=1001 pid=66632 comm=sh file=/bin/sh
uid=1001 pid=66633 comm=id file=/usr/bin/id
uid=1001 pid=66634 comm=cat file=/usr/bin/cat
blocks.caption: Real run: bpftrace 0.20.2, kernel 6.12 (arm64), privileged container. Lines from the container runtime were filtered out.

blocks.md:
**Why sensors moved here.** Compared with audit, the filtering runs *inside* the kernel on the kernel's own data structures, so a sensor sends user space only the events it wants, with richer context (container, parent chain, file paths). [Microsoft documents this move](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-endpoint/linux-support-ebpf) for Defender for Endpoint on Linux: its eBPF sensor replaced auditd as the supplementary event source, citing performance, stability and less "AuditD-related log noise", and since agent version 101.2408.0000 auditd is no longer supported for that role.

**And why defenders watch eBPF too.** Root can load eBPF programs, so an intruder with root can as well, and the verifier will not judge their intent. Record every program load: `bpf()` command 5 is `BPF_PROG_LOAD` (in the kernel's `enum bpf_cmd`), and an audit rule can match on it.

blocks.code:
$ auditctl -a always,exit -F arch=b64 -S bpf -F a0=5 -k bpf_prog_load
$ bpftrace -e 'tracepoint:sched:sched_process_exec { @[comm] = count(); }'   # root, login uid alice
$ ausearch -k bpf_prog_load -i | grep '^type=SYSCALL'
type=SYSCALL ... : arch=aarch64 syscall=bpf success=yes exit=3 a0=BPF_PROG_LOAD ...
  auid=alice uid=root ... comm=bpftrace exe=/usr/bin/bpftrace key=bpf_prog_load
... (3 program loads in total for this one-liner)
blocks.caption: Real run. a0 is the first argument of bpf(), the command. bpftrace also made over a hundred other bpf() calls (maps, BTF (BPF Type Format) type data, feature probes), which is why this rule filters on a0=5.

blocks.md: Two hardening knobs from the prereq course matter here: `kernel.unprivileged_bpf_disabled` keeps eBPF a root-only tool, and lockdown integrity mode (lesson 6) still lets your sensors attach kprobes while blocking BPF writes to user memory.

eBPF lets a verified program run at a kernel hook and filter events in the kernel. That makes it the basis of modern Linux sensors. The verifier checks safety, not intent, so treat every BPF program load as a security event.

blocks.question: What does the eBPF verifier guarantee about a program?
options: That it is not malicious
That it is signed by the kernel vendor
That it only reads, never writes
That it will finish and only access memory it is allowed to, so it cannot crash or hang the kernel
blocks.explain: The documentation is explicit: the verifier is a safety tool, not a security tool. A program that safely reports every password typed would pass it. Who may load programs is controlled by CAP_BPF, root and unprivileged_bpf_disabled.

blocks.question: Why do EDR vendors prefer eBPF sensors over reading auditd output?
options: eBPF works without root
Filtering runs in the kernel close to the event, so fewer, richer events reach user space, without a kernel module
Audit cannot record execve
eBPF programs cannot be detected
blocks.explain: In-kernel filtering cuts the volume that crosses into user space and gives access to kernel context; no custom module is needed. Audit can record execve fine (lesson 8), and eBPF loads are visible, as the audit rule above shows.

lessons.title: Falco: turning the system call stream into alerts

blocks.md:
eBPF gives you raw events. A detection tool adds the rules. **Falco** is "a cloud native security tool that provides runtime security across hosts, containers, Kubernetes, and cloud environments", originally created by the company Sysdig and now a graduated project of the **CNCF** (Cloud Native Computing Foundation): [accepted on 10 October 2018, graduated on 29 February 2024](https://www.cncf.io/projects/falco/). Its docs summarise what it does in three steps: parse Linux system calls from the kernel at runtime, assert the stream against a rules engine, alert when a rule is violated.

To collect events Falco loads a **driver**. The default is the **modern eBPF probe**; a kernel module is the alternative. Falco keeps state about processes, open files and containers, so a rule about a single `openat` call can also ask about the process's parent, its container image and its login uid.

blocks.title: One event through Falco: cat /etc/shadow in a container

scenes.caption: cat opens /etc/shadow for reading. The probe copies the event out of the kernel into a ring buffer.
Falco adds context it has been tracking: which container (lht22, image ubuntu:22.04), the parent process, the login uid.
The rule Read sensitive file untrusted asks: is it an open for read, is the file sensitive, and is the program not on a trusted list? All true.
Falco prints the rule's output with fields filled in, at priority Warning, and sends it on. Nothing was blocked: Falco detects, it does not enforce.

blocks.md: **A rule is YAML.** It has at least `rule` (a name), `desc`, `condition` (a Boolean expression over event fields), `output` (the alert text with `%field` placeholders) and `priority`. Two helpers keep conditions readable: a **macro** is a named, reusable piece of condition, and a **list** is a named set of values. Here is the real default rule from Falco 0.45.2, shortened.

blocks.code:
- macro: open_read
  condition: (evt.type in (open,openat,openat2) and evt.is_open_read=true
              and fd.typechar='f' and fd.num>=0)

- list: sensitive_file_names
  items: [/etc/shadow, /etc/sudoers, /etc/pam.conf, /etc/security/pwquality.conf]

- macro: sensitive_files
  condition: >
    (fd.name in (sensitive_file_names) or
      fd.directory in (/etc/sudoers.d, /etc/pam.d))

- rule: Read sensitive file untrusted
  condition: >
    open_read
    and sensitive_files
    and proc_name_exists
    and not proc.name in (user_mgmt_binaries, userexec_binaries, package_mgmt_binaries,
     cron_binaries, read_sensitive_file_binaries, shell_binaries, hids_binaries, ...)
    and not ansible_running_python
    ...
  output: Sensitive file opened for reading by non-trusted program | file=%fd.name
    ... user=%user.name user_loginuid=%user.loginuid process=%proc.name
    parent=%proc.pname command=%proc.cmdline terminal=%proc.tty
  priority: WARNING
  tags: [maturity_stable, host, container, filesystem, mitre_credential_access, T1555]
blocks.caption: From /etc/falco/falco_rules.yaml in the falcosecurity/falco image. Most of the condition is exclusions for programs that legitimately read these files.

blocks.code:
$ docker exec lht22 cat /etc/shadow > /dev/null
Warning Sensitive file opened for reading by non-trusted program | file=/etc/shadow
  gparent=initd ... evt_type=openat user=root user_uid=0 user_loginuid=-1 process=cat
  proc_exepath=/usr/bin/cat parent=containerd-shim command=cat /etc/shadow terminal=0
  container_id=58f0189c5a62 container_name=lht22 container_image_repository=ubuntu
  container_image_tag=22.04 ...
blocks.caption: Real alert from Falco 0.45.2 with the modern eBPF probe on kernel 6.12 (timestamp removed, wrapped).

blocks.md: **Writing your own.** Default rules cover common patterns; your fleet's persistence paths deserve rules of their own. This rule fires when anything other than the package manager or systemctl writes a file under `/etc/systemd/system`, the location used by ATT&CK T1543.002. It was loaded from `/etc/falco/rules.d/` and triggered for real. The condition's `not proc.name in (unit_writer_binaries)` is an **allowlist**: it trades a blind spot (an attacker who uses `systemctl edit`) for less noise, and you should know you made that trade.

blocks.code:
- list: unit_writer_binaries
  items: [dpkg, rpm, systemctl, apt, dnf]

- rule: Unit file written outside package manager
  desc: A process wrote a file under /etc/systemd/system (ATT&CK T1543.002).
  condition: >
    evt.type in (open, openat, openat2) and evt.is_open_write=true
    and fd.typechar='f'
    and fd.name startswith /etc/systemd/system/
    and not proc.name in (unit_writer_binaries)
  output: >
    Unit file written | file=%fd.name process=%proc.name
    command=%proc.cmdline parent=%proc.pname user=%user.name
    loginuid=%user.loginuid container=%container.name
  priority: WARNING
  tags: [host, container, persistence, T1543.002]

# triggered by: cp /tmp/updater.service /etc/systemd/system/updater.service
Warning Unit file written | file=/etc/systemd/system/updater.service process=cp
  command=cp /tmp/updater.service /etc/systemd/system/updater.service parent=bash
  user=root loginuid=-1 container=lht22 ...
blocks.caption: Real rule and alert (the desc was shortened to one line here).

blocks.md: **Noise is the real enemy.** During the same session the default rule *Drop and execute new binary in container*, at priority Critical, fired every time we ran `auditctl` in the lab container, because we had installed auditd after the container started, so the binary was not part of the image. For a production container that pattern is a classic sign of an intruder; for a lab or debugging container it is normal. The rule's own description says so and suggests an allowlist of images. Tuning per environment, as in Logging and detection engineering, is part of running Falco.

Falco watches system calls. In April 2025 the security company ARMO showed a proof-of-concept rootkit that does its file and network work through io_uring (lesson 6), and reported Falco's default rules did not see it. Lesson 13 covers what that means for every syscall-based sensor.

Falco = driver (modern eBPF by default) + state + YAML rules (condition, output, priority, macros, lists). It detects, it does not block. Every exclusion you add is a deliberate blind spot; write it down.

blocks.question: A Falco rule condition ends with `and not proc.name in (backup_tools)`. An attacker copies their tool to /tmp/rsync and runs it. What happens?
options: Falco blocks the process
The rule still fires because Falco checks file hashes
If rsync is in backup_tools, the rule is skipped: proc.name is just the program name, which the attacker chose
Falco crashes
blocks.explain: Name-based allowlists match whatever name the process has. Prefer stronger fields where possible (proc.exepath, container image, parent), and accept that every exclusion is a potential hiding place.

blocks.question: What is the role of a Falco macro?
options: It runs a shell command when a rule fires
It is a named, reusable piece of a condition, such as open_read, so rules stay short and consistent
It loads the kernel driver
It sets the alert priority
blocks.explain: Macros are condition fragments referenced by name; lists are named sets of values. Both let many rules share one definition, so fixing a macro fixes every rule that uses it.

lessons.title: Tetragon: filtering and enforcing inside the kernel

blocks.md:
Falco moves every interesting event to user space and decides there. **Tetragon**, part of the Cilium project (an open-source, eBPF-based networking, observability and security project), takes the other approach: it "applies policy and filtering directly in eBPF in the kernel", sending only matching events to its agent, and it can act in the kernel before the operation completes. Its docs list process execution, system call activity and I/O (file and network access) as what it detects, with Kubernetes awareness when run in a cluster.

You describe what to watch in a **TracingPolicy**, a YAML document naming a hook (here a kprobe on a kernel function), the arguments to capture, and **selectors**: filters on those arguments, plus **actions** to take on a match.

blocks.code:
apiVersion: cilium.io/v1alpha1
kind: TracingPolicy
metadata:
  name: "shadow-read-block"
spec:
  kprobes:
  - call: "security_file_permission"
    syscall: false
    args:
    - index: 0
      type: "file"   # struct file *: Tetragon resolves the path
    - index: 1
      type: "int"    # requested access: 4 is MAY_READ
    selectors:
    - matchArgs:
      - index: 0
        operator: "Equal"
        values:
        - "/etc/shadow"
      - index: 1
        operator: "Equal"
        values:
        - "4"
      matchActions:
      - action: Sigkill
blocks.caption: Written for this course from the structure of Tetragon's file_monitoring_enforce.yaml example, narrowed to one file. security_file_permission is the kernel's LSM hook for file reads and writes.

blocks.md:
**Why hook `security_file_permission` and not the `openat` system call?** This LSM hook runs deeper in the kernel, on the kernel's own file object, after the path has already been resolved. System call arguments are pointers into the calling program's memory; [Tetragon's overview warns](https://tetragon.io/docs/overview/) that syscall tracing can see data that is "incorrectly read, maliciously altered by attackers, or missing", which is the TOCTOU (time of check to time of use) race you met in the prereq course. Hooking deeper avoids it.

We ran this policy for real with Tetragon v1.8.0 in Docker and tried two reads from a container.

blocks.title: The policy in action (real run)

scenes.caption: cat asks to read /etc/shadow. The kernel calls security_file_permission with the file and MAY_READ (4).
Tetragon's eBPF program at the hook compares both arguments in the kernel. Both match the selector, so the Sigkill action fires.
The event goes to the agent with the action recorded. In the shell, cat died with status 137 (128 + 9, the SIGKILL signal number).
head reads /etc/passwd. The path does not match, the program filters it out in the kernel, and nothing is sent at all.

blocks.code:
$ docker exec lht22 bash -c 'cat /etc/shadow > /dev/null; echo "cat exit=$?"; \
                             head -c 10 /etc/passwd > /dev/null; echo "head exit=$?"'
bash: line 1:  3096 Killed                  cat /etc/shadow > /dev/null
cat exit=137
head exit=0

$ docker exec tetragon tetra getevents        # one event, shortened
{"process_kprobe": {
   "process": {"pid": 70701, "uid": 0, "binary": "/usr/bin/cat",
               "arguments": "/etc/shadow", "auid": 4294967295,
               "docker": "58f0189c5a622a06b86616103508c74", ...},
   "parent":  {"binary": "/usr/bin/bash", ...},
   "function_name": "security_file_permission",
   "args": [{"file_arg": {"path": "/etc/shadow", "permission": "-rw-r-----"}},
            {"int_arg": 4}],
   "action": "KPROBE_ACTION_SIGKILL",
   "policy_name": "shadow-read-block"},
 "time": "2026-11-23T05:38:18.432027013Z"}
blocks.caption: Real run: Tetragon v1.8.0, kernel 6.12 (arm64). The JSON is a real event, trimmed and reformatted.

blocks.md:
