**What Sigkill does and does not guarantee.** Tetragon's enforcement docs describe two mechanisms. **Override** changes a function's return value so the operation never runs and the caller gets an error; only system calls and security check functions allow it. **Signals** such as SIGKILL terminate the process synchronously, but "sending a SIGKILL signal does not always stop the operation": the docs give the example that a SIGKILL during `write()` does not guarantee the data is not written. To be sure the operation does not complete, combine Sigkill with Override.

Enforcement in the kernel is powerful and blunt. A policy typo can kill your own services across the fleet, so the usual path is to run a policy in observe-only mode (no action), read what it would have hit, and only then add actions.

A kprobe policy depends on a kernel function name and its arguments, which are not a stable interface and can change between kernel versions. Test policies against every kernel version in your fleet, and watch for the policy failing to load after a kernel update.

Tetragon filters in the kernel and can act there. Hook LSM functions such as security_file_permission rather than raw system call arguments, start in observe mode, and pair Sigkill with Override when the operation itself must not happen.

blocks.question: A Tetragon policy sends Sigkill when a process writes to /etc/passwd via a hook on the write path. An analyst says the file can no longer be modified. What is the gap?
options: Tetragon cannot watch /etc
Sigkill only works in Kubernetes
The write is blocked but no event is generated
SIGKILL ends the process, but per the docs it does not guarantee the write did not happen; add Override to make the call fail
blocks.explain: The enforcement docs are explicit: a SIGKILL during write() does not guarantee the data is not written. Override makes the checked function return an error so the operation is not performed.

blocks.question: Why does a sensor hook security_file_permission rather than reading the file name from the openat() system call arguments?
options: openat() cannot be traced
The hook sees the kernel's resolved file, which user space cannot change after the check, avoiding TOCTOU races on syscall arguments
security_file_permission runs in user space
It is faster to write in YAML
blocks.explain: Syscall arguments live in user memory and can be changed between when a sensor reads them and when the kernel uses them. The LSM hook runs on the kernel's own file object.

lessons.title: Linux EDR and fleet telemetry: what sensors see and miss

blocks.md:
An **EDR** (endpoint detection and response) agent, as Logging and detection engineering defined it, records process, file and network activity on a host and can isolate it. On Linux, EDR products and open tools are built from the parts you have now seen:

- **Audit-based**: rules in the kernel audit system, records read from auditd or directly from the netlink socket.
- **eBPF-based**: programs at tracepoints, kprobes and LSM hooks (Falco, Tetragon, and Microsoft Defender for Endpoint on Linux since it dropped auditd).

- **Kernel modules**: the older approach, with full access and full crash risk, and blocked by lockdown unless signed.
- **Query-based**: **osquery** "[exposes an operating system as a high-performance relational database](https://osquery.readthedocs.io/en/stable/)", so you can ask SQL questions such as which processes listen on which ports. For a continuous event stream it can use either the audit system or, on kernels 4.18 and newer, BPF.

Whatever the product, the questions are the same: what does it see, what does it miss, and what happens when an intruder with root goes after it.

**Blind spot 1: work that makes no system call.** io_uring lets a program queue file and network operations in a ring buffer shared with the kernel instead of calling `openat`, `connect` and so on one by one. In April 2025 ARMO published a proof-of-concept rootkit, Curing, that works entirely through io_uring. ARMO reported that Falco's rules, which rely on system call hooks, were "completely blind" to it that Microsoft Defender for Endpoint missed its test actions whether or not io_uring was used (only its file integrity monitoring flagged file changes, either way), while Tetragon could catch it only with policies on kprobes or LSM hooks rather than system calls. ARMO added that the Falco maintainers were working on a plugin for LSM hooks.

Defences, all from sources in this course: hook LSM functions or kernel functions below the system call layer (lesson 12); add audit's `io_uring` filter list, which `audit.rules(7)` documents (`-a always,io_uring -S openat,openat2 -F key=access`); and where workloads do not need io_uring, set `kernel.io_uring_disabled` (lesson 6).

**Blind spot 2: lies told in user space.** A **userland rootkit** hides by hooking library functions inside processes, for example through `/etc/ld.so.preload`, so `ps`, `ls` and `netstat` on the infected host stop showing its files, processes and sockets. Anything that asks through those hooked functions is fooled; a sensor reading the kernel's own data is not. Lesson 14 shows a real one.

**Blind spot 3: the sensor itself.** An intruder with root can stop, uninstall or blind agents. MITRE ATT&CK records that TeamTNT "disabled and uninstalled security tools such as Alibaba, Tencent, and BMC cloud monitoring agents" and searched running processes for their names first. The defender's answer is off-host: alert when a host stops sending, and treat an agent stop that is not part of a change as an incident.

blocks.title: Which sensor sees what (1 yes, 0.5 with extra rules, 0 no)

scenes.caption: Simplified, from this course's sources and our own runs. Every kernel-side sensor records ordinary execs and file writes made through system calls.
io_uring: Falco's syscall rules missed ARMO's rootkit; LSM or kprobe hooks see the operation; audit needs its separate io_uring rules.
A userland rootkit fools tools that call hooked library functions on the host. Kernel-side sensors never ask those functions.
No on-host sensor reports its own death reliably. Only an off-host check, a host that went silent, covers that column.

blocks.code:
# osquery: ask the fleet a question in SQL (illustrative query, not run here)
SELECT p.pid, p.name, p.path, l.port, l.address
FROM listening_ports AS l JOIN processes AS p USING (pid)
WHERE l.port NOT IN (22, 443);

# audit: watch io_uring file opens too (syntax from audit.rules(7))
-a always,io_uring -S openat,openat2 -F key=access

# kernel: refuse new io_uring instances where nothing needs them (kernel sysctl docs)
kernel.io_uring_disabled = 2
blocks.caption: Three layers for the blind spots above. io_uring_disabled = 2 fails io_uring_setup() for every process; 1 allows only privileged processes or members of io_uring_group.

blocks.md: Do not set kernel.io_uring_disabled fleet-wide without checking workloads: io_uring exists for performance, and some of your workloads may use it. This is a tailoring decision per host class (lesson 4).

Every sensor has a layer it watches and layers it cannot. Syscall hooks miss io_uring; host tools miss userland rootkits; nothing on the host reliably reports its own removal. Combine kernel-side sensors at LSM or kprobe level with off-host silence alerts.

blocks.question: A host has a userland rootkit that hooks libc to hide a process. Which source still shows that process?
options: ps run in an SSH session on that host
ls /proc in an SSH session on that host
netstat on that host
An eBPF sensor recording sched_process_exec in the kernel
blocks.explain: The hooked library lies to programs that call it, and shells spawned on the host are injected. The eBPF program reads kernel events, which the userland hooks never touch.

blocks.question: Your Falco deployment uses only default syscall rules. What does ARMO's 2025 io_uring research imply?
options: Falco is useless and should be removed
io_uring is only available on Windows
File and network operations done entirely through io_uring may produce no alert; add coverage below the syscall layer or restrict io_uring
Falco blocks io_uring by default
blocks.explain: Operations submitted through io_uring do not pass through the syscall hooks those rules use. Mitigate with LSM or kprobe hooks, audit's io_uring rules, or io_uring_disabled where workloads allow.

blocks.question: Which single control best covers an intruder who stops your EDR agent with root?
options: An off-host alert when a host stops sending telemetry, plus a rule for agent stop events while they still flow
A longer audit backlog
Raising the Falco priority to Critical
Running the agent with ProtectSystem=strict
blocks.explain: Once the agent is stopped, the host reports nothing, so detection must come from outside: the SIEM notices the silence. TeamTNT's documented behaviour (disabling cloud monitoring agents) is why this matters.

lessons.title: Case: Ebury, an SSH backdoor on 400,000 servers over 15 years

blocks.md:
**Ebury** is "the OpenSSH backdoor and credential stealer" that ESET, a Slovak security company, has tracked for over a decade. In 2014 ESET described it in a paper called Operation Windigo; on 14 May 2024 its researcher Marc-Etienne M.Léveillé published a follow-up, [*Ebury is alive but unseen*](https://web-assets.esetstatic.com/wls/en/papers/white-papers/ebury-is-alive-but-unseen.pdf). Its numbers explain why it belongs in a fleet course:

- About **400,000** servers compromised since 2009, nearly all Linux (the total includes roughly 400 FreeBSD and a dozen OpenBSD and SunOS servers), and more than 100,000 still compromised as of late 2023. The count comes from the operators' own records of hosts they compromised, which ESET obtained.

- One 2019 incident at a large US hosting provider covered about 2,500 physical and 60,000 virtual servers, all built the same way, so the same malware worked everywhere.
- ESET rented a server from a provider it believed was compromised and logged in once with the provider's root password; seven days later Ebury 1.8.2 was installed.

Installing Ebury requires root. Everything interesting is how the operators got root, and how they stayed invisible once there.

**How it spreads (ESET 2024).**

- **Credential reuse.** On each compromised host the operators collect `known_hosts` files (servers this host connected to) and `wtmp` login records (who connected in), then try the stolen passwords and keys on those related servers. Of 4.8 million `known_hosts` entries collected, about 2 million had hashed host names (OpenSSH's `HashKnownHosts` option); about 40% of those, roughly 800,000, were guessed or brute forced.
- **Hosting providers.** With access to a provider's infrastructure they installed Ebury on servers rented to customers, with no warning to the customers.
- **Adversary in the middle.** From compromised servers in a data centre they used ARP spoofing (from Network attacks and defences) against servers on the same segment to capture SSH credentials; more than 200 servers were targeted in 2023, including Bitcoin and Ethereum nodes.
- **Exploits.** In November 2020 they exploited Control Web Panel (a server admin web panel) via what became CVE-2021-45467 (a pre-auth file inclusion bug), and used Dirty COW (CVE-2016-5195) to gain root.

blocks.title: Where Ebury hides: one repointed link in sshd's dependencies

scenes.caption: Per ESET, libkeyutils.so.1 is a dependency of libkrb5, which both the OpenSSH client and server load. Normally the link points at the packaged library.
The most common technique: drop a malicious copy next to the real one (ESET's example ends in .2) and repoint the link. It contains keyutils plus the Ebury payload.

Since version 1.6 Ebury injects itself with LD_PRELOAD (a variable that makes the loader load a library first) into shells spawned through the compromised sshd, hooking libc so files, processes, sockets and even memory maps are hidden.
ESET's advice: check from an untampered session. systemd-run -S (systemd 240 or newer) starts a shell whose parent is PID 1, which Ebury is not in.

blocks.md:
**What an investigator on that host sees.** If you SSH in to check, your shell is a child of the infected sshd, so the rootkit is in your shell too: `ls` hides the extra library, `ps` hides the Ebury process. ESET lists ways to get a clean view: `systemd-run -S`, a physical or virtual console that does not go through OpenSSH, or (specific to Ebury) setting certain environment variables that make it stand down. Version 1.8, first seen late 2023, added new obfuscation, a domain generation algorithm (DGA: code that computes fresh server domain names over time, so blocking one name does not cut contact) and a better userland rootkit; ESET notes its own detection script may already be outdated and publishes a more generic detector and indicators on GitHub.

**A fleet check that does not trust the library.** Package verification alone is not enough. We repointed the link to an unowned copy of the real library in a lab container (no malware involved) and asked the package manager.

blocks.code:
# lab container: copy the real library, repoint the link (simulates the layout only)
$ ls -l /usr/lib/aarch64-linux-gnu/libkeyutils.so.1*
lrwxrwxrwx 1 root root    18 Nov 23 06:03 libkeyutils.so.1 -> libkeyutils.so.1.2
-rw-r--r-- 1 root root 67432 Apr  8  2024 libkeyutils.so.1.10
-rw-r--r-- 1 root root 67432 Nov 23 06:03 libkeyutils.so.1.2

$ dpkg --verify libkeyutils1; echo "verify exit=$?"
verify exit=0                        # no warning, yet the packaged link was repointed:
                                     # dpkg --verify checks file contents, not links

$ dpkg -S "$(readlink -f /usr/lib/aarch64-linux-gnu/libkeyutils.so.1)"
dpkg-query: no path found matching pattern /usr/lib/aarch64-linux-gnu/libkeyutils.so.1.2
                                     # the library actually loaded belongs to no package
blocks.caption: Real run on Ubuntu 24.04 (arm64), restored afterwards. On x86-64 the directory is /usr/lib/x86_64-linux-gnu. Run such checks from a clean session, or better, off the host against a disk snapshot.

blocks.md:
**Defender view, mapped to this course.**

- **Prevent.** SSH keys generated on the administrator's own trusted machine instead of provider-supplied root passwords, and MFA for SSH; ESET notes MFA "still isn't widely adopted for SSH" and needs third-party PAM modules. Patch (Dirty COW, CWP). Limit who can reach SSH. An immutable `/usr` (lesson 18) would refuse the dropped library outright.
- **Detect.** An audit watch on library directories or a Falco or Tetragon rule on writes under `/usr/lib` catches the drop; kernel-side exec and file events are not filtered by the userland rootkit (lesson 13). Fleet queries for "loaded library not owned by any package" and file integrity monitoring (AIDE, in the CIS benchmarks) catch the persistence.
- **Respond.** ESET is blunt: "a complete reinstallation is necessary", without reusing any keys or credentials from the server, and all credentials on it, encrypted or not, "must be regarded as compromised". Do not log in from the compromised host to anything else.

Ebury spread by reusing credentials found on compromised hosts, hid in one repointed library link, and lied to every shell started through sshd. Check from below the lie (kernel sensors, clean sessions, off-host snapshots), verify ownership of what is loaded, not just package checksums, and rebuild rather than clean.

blocks.question: You SSH into a suspected Ebury host and `ls -l /usr/lib/x86_64-linux-gnu/libkeyutils*` shows only the normal files. Why is that not reassuring?
options: Your shell was spawned by the possibly infected sshd, and Ebury's userland rootkit hooks libc in such shells to hide its files
ls cannot list symbolic links
Ebury only runs on FreeBSD
libkeyutils is not used by OpenSSH
blocks.explain: ESET documents that Ebury injects into shells spawned through the compromised OpenSSH server and hides its file, process and socket. Use systemd-run -S, a console, or an off-host check.

blocks.question: In the lab run, `dpkg --verify libkeyutils1` exited 0 while the loaded library belonged to no package. What does that teach?
options: dpkg is broken
The attack is impossible on Debian-based systems
Symbolic links are always safe
Checksum verification only covers files the package owns; an extra file plus a repointed link needs an ownership check of what is actually loaded
blocks.explain: dpkg --verify only checksums the contents of the package's regular files. The repointed link is a package file, but dpkg does not check link targets, and the added .2 file belongs to no package, so nothing is flagged. (rpm -V does report a changed link.) Asking which package owns the resolved target (dpkg -S, rpm -qf) exposes it.

blocks.question: After confirming Ebury on a server, what does ESET recommend?
options: Delete the malicious library and reboot
Rotate only the root password
Reinstall completely and treat every credential and key that was on the server as compromised
Run the detection script daily from then on
blocks.explain: ESET says a complete reinstallation is necessary, without reusing keys or credentials from the server. Cleaning in place leaves the stolen credentials valid and other persistence possibly in place.

lessons.title: Case: Kinsing and TeamTNT, cryptominers on exposed Linux hosts

blocks.md: Most Linux intrusions in the cloud are not spies; they are **cryptojacking**: running a cryptocurrency miner on someone else's machines. The money comes from CPU time, so the attackers want many hosts, quickly, and to stay on them. Two long-running groups show the whole pattern, and every step leaves a signal you have learned to collect.

**TeamTNT.** CERT-EU, the computer emergency response team for the EU's institutions, [summarised the August 2020 disclosure in a threat memo](https://cert.europa.eu/static/MEMO/2020/TLP-WHITE-CERT-EU-THREAT-MEMO-Cryptominer-steals-AWS-credentials-v1.0.pdf) dated 19 August 2020: a worm of the same name as the group behind it targeted AWS, Docker and Kubernetes, stole AWS credentials (which the AWS command-line tool stores unencrypted), reused them to spread, scanned for unsecured Docker instances, and installed the XMRig miner for the Monero cryptocurrency on at least 119 systems, including Jenkins servers (Jenkins automates software builds). [In 2021 Trend Micro found a script](https://www.trendmicro.com/en_us/research/21/c/teamtnt-continues-attack-on-the-cloud--targets-aws-credentials.html) of theirs that collected credentials from the AWS instance metadata service (an address inside each cloud VM that hands it data about itself, including temporary credentials); it counted over 4,000 infected instances, about 5% of them holding AWS customer information.

**What TeamTNT did on a host**, from its MITRE ATT&CK group entry (G0139): created a system service to run the miner via systemctl, added RSA keys to `authorized_keys`, created local privileged users, used libprocesshider to modify `/etc/ld.so.preload` and the open-source Diamorphine rootkit to hide mining, modified permissions on binaries with `chattr`, disabled iptables, removed `/var/log/syslog`, cleared shell history with `history -c`, searched for and uninstalled cloud monitoring agents, killed rival miners, and queried the instance metadata service for credentials.

**Kinsing.** Microsoft Defender for Cloud researchers wrote in January 2023 that Kinsing's two most common ways into Kubernetes clusters were **vulnerable images** (exploited applications included PHPUnit, Liferay, WebLogic and WordPress; one campaign scanned for WebLogic's default port 7001 and used CVE-2020-14882 and related bugs) and **exposed PostgreSQL** configured with `trust` authentication, which, per the PostgreSQL documentation Microsoft quotes, lets anyone who can connect log in as any database user, even a superuser. On 3 November 2023 the cloud security company Aqua Security [reported](https://www.aquasec.com/blog/loony-tunables-vulnerability-exploited-by-kinsing/) Kinsing attackers manually trying to exploit [Looney Tunables (CVE-2023-4911)](https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2023-4911), a glibc dynamic loader overflow Qualys had disclosed in October that gave root on default Fedora, Ubuntu and Debian installs, and probing the AWS metadata service.

blocks.title: One cryptojacking intrusion, and the control that breaks each step

nodes.label:
1 access: open Docker
API, old app, trust DB

6 spread
reuse keys,
scan for more

controls: patch, baseline,
audit + eBPF rules

scenes.caption: Access: the attack starts at something reachable from the internet. Prevention: no unauthenticated Docker API or database, patched images (lessons 1 to 4).
Root: a local privilege escalation or a privileged container. Prevention: patch fleets fast (lesson 16); detection: an exec as root from a web server's process tree.
Persistence: a unit file, a key, a user. Detection: the persistence and identity audit keys and the Falco unit-file rule from lessons 8 and 11 fire here.
Hiding: /etc/ld.so.preload (audit key preload), a rootkit module (blocked by module signing and lockdown, lesson 6), agents killed (off-host silence alert, lesson 13).
Mining and theft: sustained CPU, connections to pools, metadata service queries. Spreading: stolen keys used elsewhere. Each step is a second chance to catch it.

blocks.code:
# Falco default rules (falco_rules.yaml, all tagged maturity_stable) that match steps above
- rule: Clear Log Activities            # truncating log files (O_TRUNC), not rm
- rule: Search Private Keys or Passwords # hunting SSH keys
- rule: Find AWS Credentials            # hunting cloud credentials
- rule: Execution from /dev/shm         # running dropped payloads from memory-backed storage
- rule: Drop and execute new binary in container

# audit keys from lesson 8 that fire on the same steps
-w /etc/systemd/system/ -p wa -k persistence
-w /etc/ld.so.preload -p wa -k preload
-w /etc/passwd -p wa -k identity
-a always,exit -F arch=b64 -S init_module,finit_module,delete_module -k modules
blocks.caption: Rule names copied from the Falco 0.45.2 default rules file; the audit lines are lesson 8's rule set.

blocks.md:
**Defender view.**

- **Prevent.** Nothing management-related on the internet: Docker's API only on its local socket, PostgreSQL never with `trust` for remote addresses. Patch applications and base images. Apply the CIS baseline, including module signing and lockdown so a rootkit module cannot load.
- **Detect.** Audit keys or Falco and Tetragon rules on persistence paths, `ld.so.preload`, new users, and module loads; alerts on shells or downloads spawned by web servers and databases; Microsoft's alerts for this campaign were "a file was downloaded and executed" patterns. In the cloud, AWS GuardDuty (Amazon's managed threat detection service) has a finding for instance credentials used outside AWS, named by Trend Micro as a TeamTNT defence. And watch for the sensors themselves going quiet.
- **Respond.** Assume every credential on the host was taken (cloud keys, SSH keys, database passwords), rotate them, and rebuild the host from a known-good image rather than removing the miner.

"It is only a miner" is the wrong conclusion. The same access that runs XMRig stole cloud credentials and SSH keys in both cases, and TeamTNT reused them to reach new systems. Treat cryptojacking as a full root compromise.

Cryptojacking chains are short and noisy: an exposed service, a root exploit, a service file, a hiding trick, a miner. A hardened, patched baseline breaks the first two steps, and the audit and eBPF rules from this course flag the rest.

blocks.question: Your Falco alert shows a new file in /etc/systemd/system written by curl's child process on a web server, followed by high CPU. What is the right response?
options: Kill the miner process and close the ticket
Raise the Falco priority and keep watching
Uninstall Falco to reduce CPU
Treat it as a root compromise: isolate, collect evidence off-host, rotate every credential the host held, and rebuild from a known-good image
blocks.explain: Writing to /etc/systemd/system needs root, so the attacker had root. Both TeamTNT and Kinsing stole credentials, so cleaning the miner alone leaves them access. Rebuild and rotate.

blocks.question: Which single prevention would have stopped the Kinsing PostgreSQL route Microsoft described?
options: Disabling io_uring
Not exposing the database to the internet and not using `trust` authentication for remote connections
Using `trust` authentication only for 0.0.0.0/0
Running PostgreSQL with MemoryDenyWriteExecute
blocks.explain: With trust authentication anyone who can connect is accepted as any user, including superusers. Remove internet exposure and require real authentication; the other options do not touch that door.

lessons.title: Patching a fleet: automatic updates, restarts, reboots and rings

blocks.md: Linux for security called updates the single most effective defence on its checklist and showed `apt upgrade` on one host. On a fleet the hard parts are elsewhere: installing an update is not the same as *running* it, reboots cost availability, and a bad update shipped everywhere at once is its own outage.

**Step 1: install automatically.** On Ubuntu, [the `unattended-upgrades` package is installed by default](https://documentation.ubuntu.com/server/how-to/software/automatic-updates/) and applies security updates "automatically, without user interaction", once per day by default, triggered by the systemd timers `apt-daily.timer` and `apt-daily-upgrade.timer` with a random delay. Its `Allowed-Origins` list decides which repositories count (by default, the release's `-security` pocket). On Fedora and Red Hat systems, [**dnf-automatic**](https://dnf.readthedocs.io/en/latest/automatic.html) does the same from `dnf-automatic.timer`; `upgrade_type = security` limits it to updates "with an issued security advisory", and `apply_updates` defaults to false, so out of the box it only downloads.

blocks.caption: Option names and defaults from Ubuntu's server documentation and the dnf-automatic manual. when-needed reboots only when, for example, the kernel or systemd was upgraded.

blocks.md: **Step 2: make the new code actually run.** A running program keeps the old library in memory until it restarts. Ubuntu's documentation gives the example directly: after a shared library update, "every running service linked against it keeps using the old version in memory until it is restarted". `needrestart` finds those services; unattended-upgrades calls it, and from Ubuntu 24.04 it restarts affected services automatically by default, except a built-in list of services it never restarts (such as the display manager). `$nrconf{override_rc}` excludes critical services you want to restart yourself. needrestart also detects when the running kernel is older than the installed one.

**Step 3: the kernel.** A new kernel runs only after a reboot. Unattended-upgrades leaves `/var/run/reboot-required` and, if `Automatic-Reboot` is true, reboots at the configured time. **Livepatching** is the alternative for urgent kernel fixes: [per the kernel documentation](https://docs.kernel.org/livepatch/livepatch.html) it redirects calls from a vulnerable function to a fixed one "without a system reboot". It has limits: only functions that can be traced with ftrace (the kernel's built-in function tracer) can be patched, and kprobes in the original function are ignored once calls are redirected, so a sensor probing that function goes quiet. Most fleets livepatch the urgent fix and still reboot in the next window.

blocks.title: From advisory to running code on 2,000 hosts (illustrative schedule)

scenes.caption: Hour 0: the advisory lands. First question: which hosts have the affected package version? A fleet inventory answers in minutes (lesson 17).
Canaries install and restart first. You watch errors and the service's own health checks for a few hours before going wider.
Ring 1, then everyone else. Kernel fixes add a reboot inside a maintenance window, staggered so a service never loses all replicas at once.
Done means running, not installed: re-run the inventory for package versions, needrestart for stale services, and kernel version against the fixed one.

blocks.md: **Rings, automated.** Fedora CoreOS builds rings into its updater. Its agent, Zincati, takes a `rollout_wariness` value from 0.0 (most eager) to 1.0 (most conservative). [The Zincati docs describe the common setup](https://coreos.github.io/zincati/usage/auto-updates/): a few **canary** nodes at 0.0 that "receive updates as soon as they are available, can afford some downtime, and are specifically monitored in order to detect issues before they start affecting a larger fleet". Reboots can be limited to maintenance windows (the `periodic` strategy) or coordinated across the fleet with a lock manager so only a few nodes restart at once.

blocks.code:
# /etc/zincati/config.d/51-rollout-wariness.toml   (a canary node)
[identity]
rollout_wariness = 0.0

# /etc/zincati/config.d/55-updates-strategy.toml   (reboot only in weekend windows)
[updates]
strategy = "periodic"
[[updates.periodic.window]]
days = [ "Sat", "Sun" ]
start_time = "22:30"
length_minutes = 60
blocks.caption: From the Fedora CoreOS and Zincati documentation (the docs' canary example uses 0.0; their eager example uses 0.001).

blocks.md: **Cross-reference: the xz-utils backdoor** (Linux for security, "Packages and updates, and the xz-utils backdoor"), seen from the fleet. Two of its signals are fleet signals. *Exposure* was a package question: [CISA's alert advised](https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/alerts/2024/03/29/reported-supply-chain-compromise-affecting-xz-utils-data-compression-library-cve-2024-3094) downgrading to an uncompromised version "such as XZ Utils 5.4.6 Stable" and hunting for malicious activity, so the first job was a fleet query for xz 5.6.0 and 5.6.1. *Detection* was a performance anomaly: in Andres Freund's report on the oss-security list, a failed SSH login to localhost took 0.807 seconds after the backdoor versus 0.299 before, and logins used "a lot of CPU". A fleet that keeps per-service baselines (login latency, CPU per sshd session) can see that kind of change across thousands of hosts at once; one engineer noticing odd behaviour on a few Debian test installations happened to.

"Installed" is the most common false comfort in patch reports. The xz-utils and regreSSHion fixes did nothing for a daemon that kept running the old code; libraries need service restarts and kernels need reboots or livepatches. Report on what is running.

Automate installation (unattended-upgrades, dnf-automatic), automate restarts (needrestart), schedule reboots or livepatch urgent kernel fixes, roll out in rings with canaries, and verify the running version, not the package database.

blocks.question: A critical OpenSSL fix was installed on every host last night and the dashboard shows 100% patched. Which hosts are still exposed?
options: None: installed means fixed
Hosts where services linked to the old library were not restarted, since they still run the old code in memory
Only hosts without unattended-upgrades
Hosts with livepatch enabled
blocks.explain: A library update takes effect for a process only when it restarts. needrestart exists to find and restart those services. Livepatch is for the kernel, not user-space libraries.

blocks.question: Why might a team running eBPF sensors still prefer a scheduled reboot to a livepatch for a non-urgent kernel fix?
options: Livepatch requires disabling lockdown
Livepatch only works on ARM
Per the kernel docs, kprobes in the original function are ignored once calls are redirected, so a sensor probing a patched function can silently stop seeing it
Reboots are faster than livepatches
blocks.explain: The livepatch documentation lists this limitation. It is a good reason to livepatch only when the risk demands it and to reboot into the fixed kernel in the next window.

lessons.title: Case: regreSSHion across a fleet, from advisory to verified fix

blocks.md:
Linux for security explained the bug: regreSSHion (CVE-2024-6387), a signal handler race in OpenSSH's server that Qualys disclosed on 1 July 2024, a regression of a 2006 bug. This lesson is the other half: you run 2,000 Linux hosts and the advisory has just landed. What do you do, in what order, and how do you know you are done?

The facts that drive the decisions, from the primary sources:

- **Affected**: Portable OpenSSH 8.5p1 to 9.7p1 inclusive, on glibc-based Linux; fixed upstream in 9.8p1.

- **Exploitability**: OpenSSH's release notes say exploitation was demonstrated on 32-bit Linux with ASLR (address space layout randomisation, which loads code and data at random addresses) and "under lab conditions, the attack requires on average 6-8 hours of continuous connections up to the maximum the server will accept"; 64-bit was believed possible but not yet demonstrated.
- **Vendor view**: [Red Hat rated it Important](https://access.redhat.com/security/cve/cve-2024-6387), noting attackers "are forced to retry the attack thousands of times", which "generates significant noise providing defenders with an opportunity" to detect. RHEL 9 was the only affected RHEL version; RHEL 6, 7 and 8 shipped older OpenSSH that was never affected.
- **Mitigation**: `LoginGraceTime 0` removes the race but leaves sshd open to connection exhaustion, a denial of service.

**Hour 0 to 1: who is affected?** The trap is version numbers. Distributions **backport** fixes: they patch the old upstream version and bump only their own package revision. Ubuntu's notice USN-6859-1 fixed 22.04 in package `1:8.9p1-3ubuntu0.10`; the upstream part, 8.9p1, sits squarely inside the affected range. A network scanner that keeps only the upstream part of the SSH banner (Qualys's own test target announced itself as `SSH-2.0-OpenSSH_9.2p1 Debian-2+deb12u2`, with the distribution revision after the upstream version) or an inventory that keeps only the upstream version will call patched hosts vulnerable, and a team that learns to ignore those false alarms will also ignore the real ones.

The answer is a package inventory compared with the vendor's fixed versions, using the distribution's own version comparison. The script below did that for a four-host toy inventory; the output is real.

blocks.title: Package-aware triage: upstream version versus package version
blocks.code:
#!/bin/bash
# fixed openssh-server versions for CVE-2024-6387, from Ubuntu notice USN-6859-1
declare -A fixed=([24.04]="1:9.6p1-3ubuntu13.3" [22.04]="1:8.9p1-3ubuntu0.10")

while IFS=, read -r host release installed; do
  upstream=${installed#*:}; upstream=${upstream%%-*}   # 1:8.9p1-3ubuntu0.10 -> 8.9p1
  if dpkg --compare-versions "$installed" ge "${fixed[$release]}"; then
    verdict="patched"
  else
    verdict="VULNERABLE"
  fi
  printf "%-7s upstream %-6s package %-22s %s\n" "$host" "$upstream" "$installed" "$verdict"
done < inventory.csv

scenes.caption: The fixed versions come from the vendor notice, per release. They are full package versions, epoch and revision included, not upstream versions.
For display only, the script strips the epoch (1:) and revision (-3ubuntu0.10) to get the upstream version. Every host here shows a version inside 8.5p1 to 9.7p1.
dpkg --compare-versions applies Debian's real ordering rules. api-01's package is at the fixed revision, so it is patched despite its upstream number.
api-02 has an older revision of the same upstream version: genuinely vulnerable.
All four rows. A scan that keeps only the upstream version would flag four hosts; the package check flags two. Same data, half the work, and no false alarms to train people to ignore.
scenes.output:
web-01  upstream 9.6p1  package 1:9.6p1-3ubuntu13.3    patched
web-02  upstream 9.6p1  package 1:9.6p1-3ubuntu13      VULNERABLE
api-01  upstream 8.9p1  package 1:8.9p1-3ubuntu0.10    patched
api-02  upstream 8.9p1  package 1:8.9p1-3ubuntu0.6     VULNERABLE

blocks.md:
**Hours 1 to 4: reduce exposure while patches roll.** Two levers that need no new code. Network: SSH that only a bastion or VPN can reach turns "remote unauthenticated" into "remote from three addresses" (Linux for security, lesson on regreSSHion). Configuration: push `LoginGraceTime 0` through your config management to hosts that cannot be patched today, accepting the documented denial-of-service risk; remove it after patching. Because it is a desired-state change, the same playbook reverts it everywhere.

**Hours 4 to 72: patch in rings** (lesson 16), restarting sshd. A package update replaces the binary on disk, but already-running listener processes keep the old code until the service restarts; the restart is part of the fix.

**Detect while you wait.** Red Hat's point about noise is your detection: thousands of connections that never authenticate. The prereq course counted `Timeout before authentication` lines per host; on a fleet, the SIEM rule is that count per source address per hour, compared with each host's baseline.

blocks.code:
# Hour 4: did we get everyone? Re-run the inventory, then check what is RUNNING.
$ bash check.sh | grep -c VULNERABLE              # packages still old
$ needrestart -b | grep NEEDRESTART-SVC            # services still on old code (batch mode)
$ dpkg-query -W openssh-server                     # installed package version (Debian, Ubuntu)

# SIEM: pre-auth timeouts per source per host per hour (pseudo-query)
count(message = "Timeout before authentication") by host, source_ip, hour
  | where count > 10 * baseline(host)
blocks.caption: Illustrative commands, not run here. needrestart -b is its batch mode for scripts. The query is pseudo-code: write it in your SIEM's language.

blocks.md: Do not let a noisy, slow-to-exploit bug lull you: "6-8 hours" was the lab figure for one technique on 32-bit systems at disclosure. The process above (inventory, exposure, rings, verify) is the same one you will need for the next SSH bug, which may be fast.

Fleet response = package-aware inventory, immediate exposure reduction through config management, ring rollout with restarts, verification of running code, and detection of the attack's noise in the meantime. Never triage on upstream version strings alone.

blocks.question: Your vulnerability scanner reports `OpenSSH_8.9p1` on 300 Ubuntu 22.04 hosts as vulnerable to CVE-2024-6387. What should you check before escalating?
options: Nothing: 8.9p1 is in the affected range
Whether the hosts run Windows
Whether OpenSSL is installed
The installed package version against Ubuntu's fixed version 1:8.9p1-3ubuntu0.10, since Ubuntu backported the fix without changing the upstream number
blocks.explain: Distributions backport fixes. Compare the full package version with the vendor's notice (USN-6859-1 here) using the distribution's comparison rules.

blocks.question: Why did Red Hat call the attack's noise an opportunity for defenders?
options: Because it crashes the server immediately
Because it disables logging
Because exploitation needs thousands of retries, each an unauthenticated connection timing out, which shows up as bursts of 'Timeout before authentication' in logs
Because it only works over IPv6
blocks.explain: Winning a timing race takes many attempts. Each failed attempt ends with the grace-time alarm, which sshd logs. A per-source count against a baseline catches it.

blocks.question: After patching openssh-server on a host, why restart sshd?
options: The package manager requires it to finish installing
Already-running sshd processes keep executing the old code until the service restarts
To regenerate host keys
To reset LoginGraceTime
blocks.explain: Replacing the file on disk does not change code already loaded in memory. needrestart or an explicit restart makes the fix real.

lessons.title: Immutable OS images: rebuild instead of repair

blocks.md:
Everything so far assumes hosts are *mutable*: you log in, packages change files in place, and you scan afterwards to see what drifted. An **immutable** operating system flips that. The OS is built once as an image, the system part is read-only at runtime, and updates replace the whole image instead of editing it. Drift in the OS has nowhere to happen, and neither does much of an intruder's persistence.

Two open-source examples show the pattern:

- **Fedora CoreOS** uses OSTree, [whose documentation describes](https://ostreedev.github.io/ostree/introduction/) "atomic transitions between parallel-installable read-only filesystem trees" and sums up its design as "git for operating system binaries". The Zincati agent fetches new versions and `rpm-ostree` switches between on-disk deployments at boot, so an update or a rollback is one reboot.
- **Bottlerocket**, a Linux distribution for hosting containers built at Amazon, lists as security features: automated security updates using "two partition sets and an active/passive flip", an immutable root filesystem backed by dm-verity, a stateless tmpfs (memory-backed) `/etc`, no shell or interpreters in production builds, SELinux enforcing, kernel lockdown in integrity mode, and Secure Boot.

**dm-verity** is a device-mapper target (device-mapper is the kernel's layer for virtual block devices) that "[provides transparent integrity checking](https://docs.kernel.org/admin-guide/device-mapper/verity.html)" of a read-only block device: every block is checked against a tree of cryptographic hashes whose root is trusted. Bottlerocket's root filesystem is read-only and "cannot be directly modified by userspace processes", and the kernel is configured to restart if corruption is detected, so the node fails closed. Bottlerocket's docs add the honest caveat: without Secure Boot, an attacker with full access to the disk could alter both the data and the verity metadata.

Configuration is not edited in files either. On Bottlerocket, `/etc` is rebuilt from templates at every boot using settings from an API, so a change made by hand (or by an intruder) to a file in `/etc` disappears at reboot.

blocks.title: An A/B image update with rollback (simplified)

scenes.caption: The host runs image v41 from partition A, read-only. Partition B holds the previous image.
The agent downloads v42 and writes it to the inactive partition B. Nothing on the running system changes.
At the next allowed reboot the bootloader flips to B. The whole OS changes at once, never half-updated.
If v42 fails its health checks, flip back to A: rollback is the old image, untouched. Compare a failed package upgrade halfway through.

blocks.md:
**What it changes for the threats in this course.**

- **Ebury-style library drops** (lesson 14) need to write into `/usr/lib`. On a read-only, verity-checked root, that write fails; OSTree deploys the OS as a read-only tree.
- **TeamTNT-style persistence** (lesson 15) in `/etc/systemd/system` or `/etc/ld.so.preload` does not survive a reboot when `/etc` is generated at boot. Writable areas remain (Bottlerocket keeps `/var` and `/opt` on a separate local filesystem), so they become the places your audit and eBPF rules focus on.
- **No shell** removes the interpreter an attacker usually needs to chain tools together after getting code execution, as Bottlerocket's docs argue.
- **Patching** (lesson 16) becomes "ship a new image": the CIS baseline, sysctl values, unit sandboxing and audit rules are baked in and tested once, then rolled out in rings.

**What it costs.** Debugging without a shell needs a separate admin container; agents (including your EDR) must run as containers or be built into the image; and workloads that expect to `apt install` at runtime have to change.

blocks.title: Where an intruder's change can persist across a reboot (simplified)

scenes.caption: Mutable host: every location persists (1 = survives reboot). Only detection and baselines tell you something changed.
Bottlerocket-style host: read-only verity root, /etc rebuilt each boot, lockdown requires signed modules. Writable local storage like /var remains, so watch it.

blocks.md: Immutable does not mean uncompromisable. A remote bug still gives an attacker code execution in memory until the next reboot, and writable areas still persist. Keep runtime telemetry; immutability shrinks persistence, not intrusion.

Immutable images make the OS read-only and replace it whole: drift and most persistence disappear, patching becomes shipping a tested image, and runtime telemetry focuses on the few writable areas. The price is new ways to debug and to run agents.

blocks.question: On a Bottlerocket node an attacker with code execution writes a new unit file to /etc/systemd/system. What happens at the next reboot?
options: It runs at boot as root
It is gone: /etc is a memory-backed filesystem rendered from API settings at each boot
The node refuses to boot
dm-verity deletes it immediately
blocks.explain: Bottlerocket documents a stateless tmpfs /etc whose files are generated from templates on every boot, so hand edits do not persist. dm-verity protects the root filesystem, not /etc.

blocks.question: Bottlerocket documents dm-verity on its root filesystem but says the protection is incomplete unless Secure Boot is enabled. Why?
options: dm-verity only works on ARM
Secure Boot speeds up hashing
dm-verity needs Secure Boot to mount
Without verified boot, an attacker with raw disk access could change both the filesystem and the hash metadata that verity trusts
blocks.explain: Verity checks blocks against a trusted root hash. If what supplies that trust (the boot chain) can be replaced, so can the hashes. Secure Boot anchors the chain.

lessons.title: Putting it together: a fleet plan, and where to practise

blocks.md:
Here is the course as a plan you could start on Monday, in the order that removes the most risk per week of effort.

1. **Inventory.** Know every host, its distribution, kernel and package versions. Every incident in this course began with "which hosts are affected?" (xz-utils in Linux for security; regreSSHion in lesson 17).
2. **Patch pipeline.** Automatic security updates, needrestart, reboot windows, rings with canaries, and verification of running versions (lesson 16).
3. **Baseline as code.** CIS Level 1 through ComplianceAsCode, tailored per host class, waivers with owners and expiry dates, scanned on a schedule (lessons 2 to 4).

4. **Kernel and services.** Lockdown integrity, module signing, verified sysctl values, and `systemd-analyze security --threshold` in CI for every unit you ship (lessons 5 and 6).
5. **Telemetry.** Keyed audit rules for identity, privilege, persistence and modules, ended with `-e 2`; a kernel-level eBPF sensor; everything shipped off the host; alerts on lost events and silent hosts (lessons 7 to 13).
6. **Images.** Where the platform allows, move to immutable images so the baseline and sensors are built in (lesson 18).

blocks.md:
**Where to practise (legally).** Only test systems you own or have written permission to test. Everything in this course runs on a laptop.

- **Your own lab.** Two or three Ubuntu or Fedora virtual machines are enough. Scan one with OpenSCAP's CIS profile, tailor it, fix the failures with the generated Ansible, and rescan. Load the lesson 8 audit rules, run the intrusion story, and find it with `aureport -k --summary`. Install Falco and Tetragon from their docs and write the unit-file rule and the shadow policy yourself; run Tetragon policies without actions first.
- [pwn.college Linux Luminarium](https://pwn.college/linux-luminarium/): a free dojo that gently teaches the Linux command line and core Linux concepts.

- [OverTheWire Bandit](https://overthewire.org/wargames/bandit/): a beginner wargame over SSH that drills the shell and file permissions behind every check here.
- [Blue Team Labs Online](https://blueteamlabs.online/): a gamified platform for defenders, with scenario-based investigations in incident response, forensics, security operations and threat hunting (free and paid tiers).
- [CyLab Security Academy](https://cylabacademy.org/) (formerly picoCTF, Carnegie Mellon University): the former picoCTF platform, with challenges in general skills (terminal and bash) and forensics.

Inventory, patch, baseline, sandbox, watch, rebuild. Each is ordinary engineering on its own; run together as a loop on every host, they turn a fleet from 2,000 separate risks into one system you can measure.

blocks.question: You can do only one thing this quarter for a 2,000-host fleet with no automation. Which gives the most risk reduction per effort, based on this course's cases?
options: Write custom Tetragon enforcement policies for every service
Build a package inventory and an automated, ring-based patch pipeline that verifies running versions
Move every host to an immutable OS
Apply CIS Level 2 to every host at once
blocks.explain: Every case here needed either 'who is affected' answered fast or a patch applied everywhere, and inventory plus patching underpins the rest. Level 2 everywhere at once risks outages; immutable images and custom enforcement are later steps.

blocks.question: Which statement about this course's tools is accurate?
options: OpenSCAP blocks attacks in real time
Falco enforces policy by killing processes by default
auditd and eBPF sensors make patching unnecessary
Assessment tools (OpenSCAP) find drift from a baseline; telemetry tools (audit, Falco, Tetragon) record or act on what happens; neither replaces patching
blocks.explain: Assessment compares configuration with the baseline on a schedule. Telemetry watches activity; Tetragon can also enforce. None of them removes a vulnerability; patching and rebuilding do.
